data.title: The West is hooked on Chinese drugs but they could save your life
data.description:
Sir Keir Starmer’s decision to invite Sir Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca’s chief executive, to Beijing at the beginning of the year was a textbook piece of modern diplomacy.

The then-prime minister’s attempt to revive economic cooperation rested on a knockout deal that went beyond the usual warm words. Sir Pascal, a sworn Sinophile and one of the biggest cheerleaders of Chinese innovation, was only too happy to oblige.

Within hours of Sir Keir’s arrival, AstraZeneca had unveiled a plan to invest $15bn (£11bn) in China, building on its existing medical manufacturing and research capabilities in Beijing, Shanghai, Wuxi, Taizhou and Qingdao.

AstraZeneca’s pledge was the marquee announcement of Sir Keir’s trip. Sir Pascal said the “landmark investment” marked the next chapter for the company in China. For the politburo, it was further proof that their plan to turn China into a global pharmaceuticals leader has worked.

In the West, China has long been dismissed as little more than a dealer in cheap copycat medicines – both legal and illegal – and increasingly knockoffs too, such as unlicensed GLP-1 weight loss medication.

This portrayal no longer bears scrutiny, however. In recent years, the Chinese pharmaceutical industry has undergone a remarkable reinvention. Western industry leaders view it as a bona fide drug superpower at the forefront of discovery.

China controls an exciting pipeline of groundbreaking medicines and occupies a growing role as a globally important venue for clinical trials.

But for now, cooperation between East and West suits both sides. European and American drugmakers have rushed to embrace Chinese research, forging multi-billion licensing deals. Those with the appetite have opened their own labs and even set up manufacturing outposts.

Chinese science is now “the best in the world” and ignoring it is not an option, says one European pharmaceuticals chairman.

Few have led the charge as enthusiastically as Sir Pascal, AstraZeneca’s swashbuckling French boss. China is now its second-biggest market. Meanwhile GSK, the UK’s other national drug champion, has struck a series of partnerships with Chinese labs to licence promising drugs outside the country.

These relationships are critical for China’s pharmaceuticals industry, providing access to the lucrative markets that fund innovation. At home, their only customer is Xi Jinping, and he sets the price.

Yet this partnership is fragile. Amid growing concern in the US about the threat China’s new scientific prowess poses to drug supplies, innovation and even national security, industry executives fear an iron curtain will be drawn.

Drugs may be the next front in the superpower trade war that has already drawn in telecoms equipment, semiconductors, electric vehicles, rare earth minerals and solar panels.

For Europe, including Britain’s pharmaceutical giants AstraZeneca and GSK, the looming nightmare is that an American administration will sooner or later use its economic muscle to effectively outlaw their cooperation with China.

One senior figure says the possibility of a sweeping American crackdown is “probably the one question that keeps me awake at night”.

China’s rapid scientific progress

Dr Zhao Hong, a renowned Chinese cancer specialist, shocked thousands of Communist Party delegates in March last year: a Guangzhou-based biotech firm had developed a cancer drug that had outperformed the world’s bestselling equivalent in clinical trials.

The work of China’s Akeso Biopharma, lung cancer drug ivonescimab had shown that it could delay non-small-cell lung cancer progression for five months longer than US giant Merck’s Keytruda treatment – the world’s bestselling prescription drug in 2025.

The success of ivonescimab was hailed as a breakthrough moment for China’s pharmaceutical industry.

“China is at the best time of its biopharmaceutical sector’s development,” Hong told state media at the annual Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.

The speed with which China is catching up in pharmaceuticals and biotech is astonishing.

By 2024, China had 1,255 drugs at the research stage, a nearly eight-fold jump in less than a decade. America had 1,441 – a 15pc rise – while the total in Europe had shrunk slightly to 400.

Experts attribute the leap to a fundamental shift in how the industry was perceived by the Chinese regime.

One veteran UK executive recalls how when he first used to visit China in the late 1990s, it was to complain about “counterfeits and pharmaceuticals that were really dangerous”. Today, China is seen as “a golden opportunity”, he says.

“They have moved deliberately to be at the leading edge of science,” he adds.

Beijing has provided vast support in the form of scores of state-financed biotechnology parks equipped with advanced laboratories and heavily subsidised hardware, together with a sweeping overhaul of the regulatory system beginning in 2015.

A study by Prof Yimin Cui, of Peking University, and colleagues found that the time taken to approve a drug for human trials fell to 87 days after the reforms, from 501 days previously.

Chinese researchers are helped by the sheer size of the country’s population – last counted at more than 1.4 billion – says Freddy Yip, a corporate lawyer at Cooley.

“In the US, it may take a long time to recruit sufficient patients, but in China, you have access to lots of different patients with different kinds of diseases, including many rare diseases,” Yip says.

Sir Pascal has said this combination of scientific capability and rapid execution – “China speed”, as he has called it – can help to dramatically accelerate drug development.

One of China’s leading biotech venture capitalists estimates clinical trials are “two thirds cheaper and half as quick in China”.

Progress has been spurred by a massive increase in spending on research and development – leaping from $35m in 2015 to $15bn in 2023 – and a “reverse brain drain” in which thousands of foreign-educated Chinese scientists and entrepreneurs have returned home, according to Porsche Consulting.

Chinese scientists are now at the vanguard of treatment for cardiovascular diseases and cancer, as well as spearheading drug development for metabolic conditions and neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s, among many others.

Alarm bells in Washington

Mere months before Sir Pascal was lending heft to Sir Keir’s Beijing bridge-building mission, the Frenchman was being warmly welcomed at the Oval Office by Donald Trump.

Thanking the US president for welcoming him “in this beautiful office”, Sir Pascal was armed with another crowd-pleasing announcement: a pledge to cut drug prescription prices in the US, after Trump had accused other countries of “freeloading” at the expense of Americans.

Sir Pascal went further as well, unveiling a $50bn plan to expand the company’s existing operations in the US. In return, AstraZeneca received a three-year exemption from tariffs.

Privately, AstraZeneca executives acknowledge it was also an attempt to ward off growing concern in the White House about the deepening of ties with China.

“We are cognisant of some of the more hawkish commentary [from US politicians]. It is a delicate balancing act, and we are treading a fine line by recognising what the US is trying to achieve,” an insider says.

Yet, for all Washington’s alarm, dependency has become more pronounced, not less. Western companies have piled into the country, hoovering up clinical trial data and striking licensing deals to develop Chinese medicines outside the mainland, which they hope can then be used to treat patients across the developed world.

“This is the golden age of science and China is white-hot right now,” an industry source says.

Deal activity is being driven by anxiety among European and US companies as their pipeline of drugs peters out.

America’s biotech industry faces the alarming prospect of an estimated $350bn worth of medicines – equivalent to roughly one fifth of projected global prescription-drug revenue – losing patent protection by the end of the decade.

When patents run out, generic rivals are allowed to gatecrash the market, jeopardising sales.

Few have led the way with the verve that AstraZeneca has demonstrated.

Sir Pascal’s Beijing announcement was accompanied by a boast that it had signed 16 global licensing agreements with 15 Chinese partners since 2023 alone – thought to be the most of any overseas pharmaceuticals multi-national.

GSK hasn’t been far behind. Last year, the company struck an alliance with local giant Hengrui Pharma to develop a dozen new medicines outside the mainland. The value of the deal could eventually total $12bn.

The agreements are part of an industry-wide surge in deals totalling $138bn last year – a nearly tenfold jump since 2021 – according to data provider PharmCube. 2026 is expected to be another record.

Deal flow shows little sign of slowing.

A fortnight ago, GSK unveiled a $1.3bn pact with Hutchmed, a Hong Kong-based biopharmaceuticals company with research facilities in Shanghai, for the bulk of the licensing rights to what it called “first in-class” cancer treatments.

Brewing geopolitical storm

Amid the feeding frenzy, concern in Washington has turned to outright hostility in some quarters.

In December last year, Trump signed into law the Biosecure Act, a move widely seen as a sharp escalation in tensions and the moment the longstanding strategic rivalry between the US and China spilt into the biotechnology arena.

The act prevents US companies reliant on federal contracts and funding from working with Chinese biotech firms with ties to the Chinese military and any deemed to pose a national security risk. It also bars Chinese companies from accessing US government funding themselves.

US biotechnology companies with federal contracts are now engaged in a mad dash to purge their supply chains of equipment obtained from any Chinese biotechnology firms on the banned list.

Next up is the Biotech Investment National Security Act. Though not yet signed into law, it will subject licensing deals involving Chinese companies to national security reviews.

Though technically a screening mechanism rather than a ban on licensing Chinese drugs, it will effectively function as one, says Craig Garthwaite, a professor at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

There is also pressure to bar the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) from accepting Chinese trial data, amid concerns about their reliability. The FDA has repeatedly rejected one of Hengrui’s cancer drugs, citing questions about quality control at its manufacturing sites.

As one senior City figure puts it: the White House has conjured up other reasons to “erect a wall around China”.

AstraZeneca’s attempt to navigate this geopolitical storm by investing in both China and the US divides opinion. Some see it as an inspired way to keep both Washington and Beijing happy at the same time.

“I think Pascal has been very smart in not allowing anybody to question his US credentials. He’s playing his cards very wisely,” the boss of a rival company says.

Others see it as a high-stakes gamble from a company that is more exposed than most of its competitors and has learnt the hard way the risks that come from operating in China.

Leon Wang, the former head of its Chinese operations, is awaiting trial on charges of illegal trading, unlawful collection of personal information and medical insurance fraud, alongside another former employee, having been arrested in 2024.

If the saga made Sir Pascal reconsider his appetite for doing business in China, there is little sign of it.

Alongside licensing deals potentially worth tens of billions of dollars, it has around 17,000 employees in China, two “global strategic” research and development centres in Beijing and Shanghai, and four advanced manufacturing sites in Wuxi, Taizhou, Qingdao and Beijing.

China is now AstraZeneca’s second-largest market after the US, accounting for roughly 12pc of the company’s global turnover, and its Chinese facilities supply more than 70 markets worldwide.

In a written submission to the Commons business and trade select committee in July, AstraZeneca described co-operation with China as a “win-win”.

But as one investor with extensive interests in China points out: “If you’re a big pharma company with a significant proportion of your licensing spend coming from China and the tap suddenly gets turned off, that’s obviously a problem.”

Europe’s wary response

Despite sharply rising tensions, there are concerns that European policymakers are still a long way off from having a coherent industrial strategy that addresses the China question.

Having been slow to react to the threat that cheap Chinese manufacturing poses to the continent’s steelmakers, solar panel producers and its car industry, the risk is that the pendulum swings too far the other way and Brussels takes a similarly antagonistic approach in trying to shut China out of other sectors, such as pharmaceuticals.

Calls by Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, for tougher trade measures against Beijing have been interpreted in some circles as a signal that EU-China relations are close to a tipping point after years of resistance to anti-Chinese duties from the continent’s car giants.

Yet, a senior industrialist says Europe lacks the “economic counterweight to be able to exclude China”.

“I don’t necessarily think it’s good in the long term for the US to do so, but I think it’s very dangerous for Europe,” he adds.

“We need a more nuanced industrial strategy that seeks Chinese expertise and cost effectiveness, and to somehow bring some of the economic benefit of that into Europe,” he says.

Such sentiment echoes a growing willingness among car manufacturers to partner with Chinese counterparts amid an onslaught of imports. Nissan’s decision to share its Sunderland plant with Chery, one of China’s largest car exporters, is expected to be among the first of many similar tie-ups.

Some believe the growing divide between Washington and Beijing because of pharmaceuticals may even present an opportunity for Europe.

“I’m sure Europe would be more than happy to take Chinese-developed products that are sold to them at a lower price than what they might otherwise get from the United States,” Garthwaite says.

As Brussels bureaucrats try to agree on a co-ordinated approach, the rhetoric, particularly among some influential Republicans, continues to harden.

Chris Klomp, a top lieutenant of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, has likened the situation to “a war”.

Anxiety has been heightened by a so-called “hot mic” incident at a Beijing military parade late last year, in which Vladimir Putin and Xi were overheard discussing the possibility that humans could live to 150 years old, thanks to advances in biotechnology.

Some China hawks saw it as further evidence that the US risked falling behind in the global race for domination in advanced science.

The Council on Foreign Relations, an influential American think tank, has called for reliance on China’s biotech know-how to be treated as a strategic vulnerability akin to critical minerals.

“The US (and just about every other nation) faces a growing risk that China will deliberately withhold essential pharmaceutical inputs as a tool of economic or political coercion … as China has done with rare-earth critical minerals,” it warned in June.

The Atlantic Council, another US think tank with a history of shaping American foreign policy, points out that the US is reliant on China for three quarters of some imported drugs and as much as 99pc of some raw materials that are critical to the production of certain key medicines.

What’s more, China’s 2020 export control law and 2021 biosecurity law “grant broad authority to weaponise pharmaceutical exports”, it said recently.

‘All in or all out’

AstraZeneca declined to comment on its position, but there are signs it is more nervous than it is willing to acknowledge.

It emerged in August that the company had held detailed discussions with American rival Bristol Myers Squibb about a potential £300bn mega-merger.

In seeking to substantially deepen its US footprint, AstraZeneca may have concluded that the best chance it has of escaping any crackdown is if the company can demonstrate it is willing to take action to address Trump’s demands for the “reshoring” of pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Radical corporate restructuring plans have also been explored in China. AstraZeneca previously looked at the possibility of carving out its Chinese business into a separate legal entity and listing it on the Shanghai stock exchange. Though nothing came of those plans, they were seen as an attempt to insulate it from mounting geopolitical tensions.

GSK, meanwhile, sees no reason for such drastic action. Publicly, all a spokesman is willing to say is that it has “a longstanding presence in China, to make sure patients can access our medicines and vaccines”.

“China is also increasingly a source of cutting-edge biopharma innovation, and we have established several important collaborations for potential new treatments in oncology, respiratory, immunology and inflammation,” the spokesman adds.

However, like AstraZeneca, it too has fallen foul of Beijing after the company was engulfed in a bribery scandal in 2014.

GSK was found guilty of bribing Chinese doctors and hospitals to prescribe its medical products and was forced to pay a record $490m fine.

That ordeal prompted GSK bosses to take a much more cautious approach in which its activities were limited to strict licensing deals rather than the asset-heavy approach of others, such as AstraZeneca.

“It [GSK] went through a very difficult time in China. The experience damaged the company immeasurably in terms of its willingness to take risks,” a City source says.

By focusing on developing local collaborations, GSK believes it can still capitalise on the opportunities in China while being “less vulnerable” than rivals who are more “asset-exposed”, an insider explains.

Yet, the same person admits it ultimately boils down to one question: “Are they [China] helping us long-term or are they harming us? And I can’t answer that, which is why we can’t afford to be all in or all out.”

Industry figures hope common sense prevails between the two superpowers.

Garthwaite acknowledges deals that come with potential national security risk should be scrutinised, while attempts to reduce American over-dependence on Chinese antibiotics are also to be applauded.

However, he says the White House needs to distinguish between drug production and drug development, which “shouldn’t be too hard”.

Another investor says patients don’t really care where the drugs come from, “as long as they’re subjected to the same trials”.

In response to a recent US ban on imports of humanoid robots, China’s foreign ministry said: “Protectionism does not make the US more competitive … it will only hurt the interests of US companies and consumers.”﻿

Yet, nor is it in China’s interests to actively undermine American science. Chinese drugmakers simply cannot afford to be shut out of Western markets, particularly the US, experts say.

“China is really vulnerable too. It has to rely on its export machine because it doesn’t have sufficient levels of internal consumption,” one analyst says.

Ultimately, industry sources admit they are at the mercy of an unpredictable Trump administration whose appetite for trade wars shows little sign of waning.

As one boardroom veteran puts it: “It’s akin to walking a tightrope – we’ll continue trying to walk it and hope we stay on.”

data.title: Europe’s richest man delays retirement until he’s 95
data.description:
Europe’s richest man, Bernard Arnault, has extended his retirement age to 95 in a move that will allow him to stay at the helm of the LVMH luxury-goods empire for another 18 years.

The extraordinary new age limit on his role as managing general partner of the holding company that controls LVMH was revealed in company filings this week in Paris.

Mr Arnault, 77, is in the throes of strengthening his family’s grip on the business that owns more than 70 luxury brands, including Louis Vuitton, Christian Dior, Dom Pérignon and Tiffany, as part of a major corporate restructuring.

A “projet de fusion” (merger plan) document lodged with France’s intellectual property office shows that the age limit of the managing general partner “is fixed at 95 years”.

That would allow Mr Arnault, whose fortune is worth an estimated £100bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, to stay in effective control of the group until 2044.

The shake-up will also see the Arnault family’s investment vehicle Agache merge with another LVMH holding company, Christian Dior SE. The new single entity will own just under 50pc of the shares, but control 66.55pc of the voting rights in LVMH.

The move is designed to streamline the family’s corporate structure and lock in multi-generational control of the group.

The 95-year age cap, first reported by Bloomberg, is 10 years older than the current limit for his chairman role at Christian Dior SE and for the chief executive position held by Mr Arnault’s 49-year-old son, Antoine.

Mr Arnault, who was born in Roubaix in 1949, has effectively controlled LVMH since 1989 after he bought a bankrupt textile group whose assets included Christian Dior.

The French businessman has a history of extending retirement ages. He first raised LVMH’s maximum age limit for its chairman and chief executive from 75 to 80 in 2022, and shareholders later approved lifting it further to 85 in April 2025.

When it went up to 80, Mr Arnault joked that the American investor Warren Buffett – who is now 96 – had asked him why he had not pushed the limit higher. Mr Buffett stepped down as chief executive of his firm, Berkshire Hathaway, only last year.

The world’s oldest billionaire is usually cited as Robert Kuok, the founder of Shangri-La Hotels, who is 103. Veteran fund manager George Soros is 96, while Rupert Murdoch, who retired as chairman of Fox Corporation and News Corp in 2023, is 95.

data.title: The BBC has ruined Christmas
data.description:
They’ve taken over Downing Street, and now the kids are in charge at the BBC. At least that’s what one must conclude from the news that much of the corporation’s Christmas content is now available on the BBC iPlayer.

Fancy an early viewing of Mark Gatiss’s annual ghost story, which, this year, is an adaptation of Charles Dickens’s The Bride’s Chamber starring Martin Freeman and Jim Broadbent? You can watch it on your phone as you hop on the bus.

Can’t wait for the Death in Paradise Christmas special or the seasonal edition of Mortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Fishing? Watch them in bed before you switch off the light. Jettisoned are the days when families up and down the land would leaf through the bumper, two-week Christmas issue of the Radio Times, circle the shows they were looking forward to most and plan their festive viewing.

That doesn’t suit the zeitgeist. None of that fuddy-duddy, appointment-to-view nonsense. Programmes have to be there when you want, wherever you want.

It’s not in the corporation’s charter to be a unifying force at Christmas. Yet it’s one of those things that the best telly has done over the years. The weddings and funerals of monarchs or major sporting events aside, there is something heart-warming about the idea of a large proportion of the nation watching the same telly at the same time over the Christmas period.

In fact, in today’s world of TikTok and doom-scrolling, brain-rotted teenagers and teen-aspiring middle-aged prime ministers, it’s never been more important for families to gather in one room and watch something together. The BBC, though, like the Government, feels it has to pander to and exacerbate this existential cultural and social crisis. Meet the young “where they are”. Give them bite-sized chunks, back to front or upside down, so long as they scratch it for just a second. Sorry, “engage with the content”.

Christmas Day can be particularly special when it is structured. In our house, the schedule goes like this: stockings, breakfast, a present-opening, church, champagne and another present, lunch, the King’s speech, walk, movie, scrambled eggs, Stilton, sleep.

My belief being those corralled into joining this routine gain a deeper experience of Christmas having been forced to go to church (makes the fizz taste better), chat to the elderly grand-rentals and strays, and then watch the same telly. And, all right, I am still in a time warp here with yearnings for a Top of the Pops Christmas special and a Bond film.

But the BBC’s iPlayer fetish, its Black Friday giveaway of everything, rips this unity to shreds. Rather than encourage the minds of the nation to focus for more than a few seconds, it chases the descent of intelligence, pricking a hole in its own balloon of proud achievement so it can crash to the ground. Screw the schedule, this is a licence-funded, pay-per-view exercise.

Except that, by jettisoning schedules, the charter dissembles. For if you are left to pick and choose everything, you are not led, via entertainment, to that which “educates and informs” (as the charter puts it). When the children run the grocer’s, they don’t care whether the kids buying ignore the apples and go straight for the sweets and vapes.

It would take particularly bold leadership to uphold some of the traditions in scheduling. But instead the BBC, tragically, ends up making its own case for de-funding.

data.title: Car bosses rail against ‘eye-watering’ cost of net zero rules
data.description:
A leading carmaker has called Britain’s electric vehicle (EV) targets “the most aggressive regulatory regime in the world”, piling more pressure on Labour to water down the rules.

Paul Philpott, president and chief executive of Kia UK, accused the Government of imposing “eye-watering” costs on the UK’s automotive industry with the controversial zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate.

He warned that the net zero regulations, along with European proposals to block UK-made cars from receiving subsidies, now posed “a real threat” to the competitiveness of domestic manufacturers.

Speaking in London on Tuesday evening, Mr Philpott said: “We have the most aggressive regulatory regime in the world. I see first-hand every day the cost of compliance – it is eye-watering.

“It has made the journey to electrification a real threat to our industry and not the positive driver of change we all want it to be.”

The EU’s “made in Europe” rules, which will exclude UK carmakers from subsidies and tax breaks under current proposals, were set to “lock us out of Europe”, he said, while post-Brexit “rules of origin” had also put domestic manufacturers at a disadvantage.

Mr Philpott added: “We need to make the UK a more attractive place in which to invest. We need action now.”

Kia is the second-best-selling car brand in the UK after Volkswagen and makes popular models including the Sportage SUV, the Picanto hatchback and the EV2 electric SUV.

Mr Philpott was speaking at an industry dinner hosted by the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT).

The lobby group has urged Labour ministers to ease the requirements of the ZEV mandate amid concerns that the headline targets are unrealistic.

Under the mandate, 33pc of new car sales must be electric in 2026, with the target rising to 80pc by 2030. A full ban on petrol and diesel cars, as well as hybrids, is then planned for 2035.

Carmakers do not have to hit these headline figures because of so-called flexibilities that are built into the scheme. However, they have complained they are spending up to £5bn a year on discounting to comply – and risk hefty fines if they do not.

Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “Mandates do not make markets: they compel supply, not demand.

“Our commitment is not in question. No industry has invested more in this transition but the costs incurred by this industry cannot continue.

“An unprofitable home market weakens the case for building here, however much we export.

“Spending resources on bridging the gap between regulation and demand is money not spent on the next model, the next factory, the next British job.

“We need full reform, not running repairs. The mandate, along with energy costs and European restrictions – effectively a triple block to investment – must change.”

A consultation on possible changes to the mandate was launched earlier this year, with options including cutting the 2030 target to 50pc, 60pc or 70pc.

But easing the mandate is not politically straightforward, with Labour ministers divided on the issue.

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, and Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, are said to be more sympathetic to industry concerns, while Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, and Ed Miliband, her predecessor and now the Foreign Secretary, are understood to be pushing back over fears it will lead to higher carbon emissions.

At the same time, EV charging companies and their investors have warned the Government that backsliding on the targets will damage confidence in the UK after many of them built infrastructure off the back of demand the mandate was expected to create.

A government spokesman said on Tuesday: “We remain committed to the phase-out of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero-emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets.

“Our consultation on the mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition.”

data.title: The truth about Black Friday ‘bargains’
data.description:
Black Friday “bargains” have been called into question after a Telegraph investigation found some of Britain’s most in-demand consumer goods could be bought for significantly less earlier this year.

Ahead of the discount day, which traditionally marks the start of the Christmas shopping season, The Telegraph has been tracking the 100 most popular products at four of Britain’s biggest retailers: John Lewis, Currys, Argos and Very.

An analysis found that, as of Wednesday, six in 10 of the most popular items for sale – in what is meant to be one of the best weeks in which to secure a bargain – were in fact more expensive than earlier in 2026.

The typical product was £28 (15pc) more expensive than the lowest price recorded for it since Jan 1, while some appeared to jump in price shortly before Black Friday.

The most striking case was Samsung’s Galaxy S26. In late October, John Lewis, Argos and Very were selling the regular black 256GB model for £629.

All four retailers then sold it for £709 as of Nov 17. Between Nov 18 and Nov 20, the price went up again to £959 at each of the four shops – a £250 jump after their Black Friday campaigns had already begun. It remained at £959 on Wednesday.

Currys said the price had gone up because of “market conditions”. Meanwhile, John Lewis said brands have their own reasons for increasing prices, such as rising production costs.

The findings will fuel concerns raised by MPs over whether shoppers can trust Black Friday discounts, and whether retailers boost prices in the run-up to the bargain season to make their deals appear more attractive.

Companies including TikTok, Amazon and John Lewis recently came under fire for declining to appear before MPs at a hearing on alleged “mis-selling of consumer items” in the run-up to Black Friday.

Liam Byrne MP, chairman of the business select committee, said at the time their refusal left it with “little option” but to deepen its investigation into whether “Black Friday is becoming yet another rip-off”.

John Lewis said that with less than a week’s notice, its senior leadership was unable to attend. It submitted a written response on the matter instead.

Martyn James, a consumer rights campaigner, has described the discount day as the “most successful psychological manipulation of shoppers in the last few decades”.

He said that retailers were aware that shoppers would be “worrying about Christmas on the horizon”, adding: “It only takes an email or advert to nudge you into an impulse buy.”

However, experts said there are some good deals out there if you know where to look.

In anticipation of Black Friday, The Telegraph used data from comparison website PriceRunner to identify the 100 most popular products sold by each retailer as of two weeks before.

There were 172 products in total, accounting for crossover between different shops, and not all of them were part of retailers’ official Black Friday promotions. The Telegraph then assessed pricing data from the beginning of 2026 for these products, excluding delivery fees.

It found that some 22 products were more than £100 more expensive than their lowest price this year, just two days before Black Friday.

Prices for Ninja’s HB150 blender rose in the run-up to Black Friday.

In early November, all four retailers were selling it for £139.99. Between Nov 11 and Nov 16, Currys, Argos and John Lewis increased the price by £50.

For both Currys and Argos, this came after their Black Friday campaigns had started. Argos, however, has since reduced the price back to £139.99.

John Lewis said its previous lower price matched a competitor’s, rather than being part of a planned promotion.

Apple’s 2025 iPad with 128GB of storage cost between £299 and £329 at Currys, John Lewis and Argos from January to June. In early July, that rose to £429 at all four retailers within four days.

It is now £399 at John Lewis, Argos and Very, with their websites telling shoppers they can “save £30” despite it selling for less earlier this year.

Currys had cut the price to £399 earlier in November, but it now stands at £429.

Apple introduced price rises on some products in late June, blaming the soaring cost of memory chips.

Both John Lewis and Argos said some of the products highlighted were not included in their Black Friday deals.

The Telegraph’s Recommended team, which tests and reviews consumer products to identify the best deal, has also manually checked 308 Black Friday deals since Monday.

It found that only 34pc met its test for a “genuine deal”, meaning they offered at least 10pc off their average price in 2026 and met the Telegraph Recommended test of quality.

Prices have also been falling in the past fortnight, and deals might improve by Friday, but the findings point towards a continuation of the same trend identified by the consumer group Which?.

Tracking thousands of daily prices on 756 home, tech and health products from eight major retailers, it found that just 22pc of deals hit their lowest price in the four-week Black Friday window last year.

A Very Group spokesman said it had great deals all year round, with Black Friday being just one of many promotional events. He added that it regularly reviews prices to ensure value is “competitive”.

A John Lewis spokesman said it had a “huge range of deals” for Black Friday, which are clearly labelled to help customers. It said items flagged in The Telegraph’s analysis were not part of this offer, “and it would be misleading to make this comparison”.

It added it matched the prices of many of its competitors and said the majority of its Black Friday deals “represented their very best price”.

An Argos spokesman said: “We work hard to offer our customers great value all year round. As this analysis shows, the majority of our most popular products are at their lowest price of the year this Black Friday.”

A Currys spokesman said it was aware customers expect genuine value from Black Friday and pointed towards its price guarantees. It said it would continue to work with suppliers to deliver competitive prices.

Samsung was also approached for comment.

data.title: ‘Santander froze my accounts in China over an impossible identity check’
data.description:
Has a company treated you unfairly? Ruth Emery, our consumer champion, is here to help. To contact Ruth, click here*.

Dear Ruth,

I am a British citizen living and working as a teacher in China. I have endured a four-month battle with Santander trying to validate my identity. My current and savings accounts plus credit card have all been blocked and I have had no end of stress trying to satisfy their increasingly ridiculous demands.

It started at the end of May, when Santander sent an email asking me to provide information to verify my identity. The bank first asked for utility bills, which I do not have as I live at the school and all utilities are paid for as part of my contract. So, I asked my manager to write a letter confirming my position and address, but this was not sufficient.

Next, they asked for a bank statement with my address and I replied that Chinese bank statements do not include addresses. That may seem odd in the UK but that is simply how it is here.

Unable to do that, I then sent a letter from the police confirming my address. Unbelievably, they refused to accept this despite me explaining that it is impossible for a foreigner to live in China without registering their address with the police.

Finally, I had to beg my manager to take me to the bank and see whether there was anything they could do. They eventually sent me a letter saying I held an account and included my address.

I sent this to Santander with a translation of the original but did not receive a reply. A week later, I called the bank and was told I needed to provide an authenticated translation as they would not accept an AI translation. I did this and then heard nothing more.

The situation then descended properly into farce when I got a phone call to tell me that if I could verify my identity with my passport and send a letter from the school confirming my address, they could try and resolve the issue. These were the very first documents I had sent them!

So, it would appear that after four months, I am back where I started.

– TH, China

Dear reader,

You have lived in China for 13 years and reckon you have been a Santander customer for at least the last two decades.

Banks do need to check who their customers are as part of anti-money laundering and “know your customer” laws. However, you have spent far too long trying to verify your name and address with Santander, with the whole process turning into a Kafkaesque nightmare.

You say you have spent a fortune calling the bank from China and your current account, savings account and credit card have all been blocked.

The bank’s actions have had a massive impact on you. You were in New Zealand when your accounts were first frozen and you were worried you’d be stranded in Auckland as no one accepted your other card, a Wise Visa.

Having said that, your Wise multi-currency debit card has been vital in helping you mitigate some of the problems you’ve had in China in terms of not being able to use your Santander accounts.

You added: “I have had a huge amount of stress, expense and wasted time trying to get in touch with companies in the UK to whom direct debits [from my Santander account] had failed.”

It seemed to me you had diligently jumped through the hoops put in front of you (or explained why it wasn’t possible in your situation) and the ball was now firmly in Santander’s court to confirm your identity and unblock your accounts.

I intervened and the bank promised to investigate. First, it reactivated Apple Pay on your credit card. Then, you had a phone call with the welcome news that all your accounts had been unfrozen.

You were offered £250 compensation but when you mentioned the expensive phone calls and huge inconvenience, Santander quickly increased it to £400, which you accepted.

A Santander spokesman said: “As part of our legal and regulatory obligations, we regularly review customer information to help keep accounts up to date and secure.

“In this case, restrictions were applied while we verified [the reader’s] overseas residency and residential address. The restrictions have now been removed and we are sorry for the delays he experienced while we carried out our review.”

You later received an email from the bank reminding you that while this matter had been resolved, “customers are generally required to be resident in the UK”. Santander added: “As you currently reside in China, any future review of your banking relationship will be considered in accordance with our policies and regulatory obligations at that time.”

I understand you may be asked for further information in future. However, you intend to jump ship from Santander to a bank account better suited for expats living in China.

– Ruth

data.title: How I turned a bland studio space into a bold, botanical two-bedroom flat
data.description:
For most commuters, catching a train is the brunt of the daily slog. But for interior designer Neil McLachlan, his commute was a mission between two far-flung corners of the world where he works on design projects: New Zealand, where he is originally from, and London, where he now lives.

“So I was searching for a central London pad to suit my work, travel and lifestyle, but I had a limited budget,” he says. “I couldn’t find anything interesting until I accidentally stumbled across this studio which I could see was brimming with potential.”

McLachlan, the founder of interior design practice Neil McLachlan Design, discovered the former photography studio on the ground floor of a large inter-war mansion block in Bloomsbury in 2018 and instantly knew he had found something special.

“The volume of the space, the lofty ceiling height, which was peppered with south-facing cloister roof lights, all held an immediate attraction,” he says. “Plus, there was the inevitable romance attached to the idea of being part of the Bloomsbury set.”

Located round the corner from Russell Square Tube and a stone’s throw from the Eurostar at St Pancras, the location ticked a lot of boxes for McLachlan. And while it had zero bedrooms, which McLachlan was determined to change, it was tucked away down a quiet side street in the heart of the city.

The flat, which he believes was originally the caretaker’s workshop, had been improved by its previous owner, a photographer who used it as a studio, who added skylights to draw in more light. But it remained a bland shell and McLachlan, who studied haute couture in Paris before moving into interiors and architecture and was a much-loved designer on New Zealand’s TV show Changing Rooms, soon got to work. 

“I wanted to create two bedrooms, including one master, and the space was just about big enough to allow for it.” He began by building a wall to break up the main space. Added to this he installed an electric fireplace, “with glowing coals that double as a fan heater”, while incorporating a large pair of antique French doors, “originally from a château”, either side, fabricating a historic patina and introducing a pleasing, symmetrical focal point to the newly designed open-plan kitchen, dining and living room.

Behind the French doors is the main bedroom, which contains a double bed, an oversized headboard and large built-in storage cupboards, which he designed “not only for practical reasons”, he explains. “I wanted to eliminate the sloping walls as much as possible.” He managed to squeeze a shower into the bathroom to create an en suite, and from his bed, the view of a beautiful mist-covered lake unfolds into the distance, thanks to a mural wallpaper from Wallsource. Its wooden jetty extends, inviting one’s eye towards the horizon, an “over-scaling” trick McLachlan used to “add a depth of view and make it feel spacious”.

Clever design and architectural tricks are employed with smart accuracy throughout this bijou home, maximising the layout and adding a feeling of roominess. A vast mirrored wall in the living room reflects light, adding to the illusion of depth. “The biggest trick is the wallpaper,” McLachlan laughs. “It adds structure and warmth, plus curation of the furniture is key. I chose perfectly proportioned pieces from the Art Deco period mixed with quirky additions.” This includes the vintage box camera now repurposed as a floor lamp and the enormous bird prints he scanned from tiny originals found in an engraving shop in Covent Garden, alongside a grand pair of brass chandeliers, which had steel struts added to support them under the roof lights.

McLachlan had a singular vision “to make the apartment feel like an old greenhouse from Kew Gardens”. To do this, he chose orangerie wallpaper from Mind the Gap. “The lush tropical plants add a surprising oasis feel. Specifically, because it’s hard to tell if you are outside looking in at the plants or inside looking out.”

The verdant jungle-style paper adds vibrancy to this London home, while the natural tones offer the perfect foil for his Lloyd Loom chairs, custom David Seyfried sofa-bed, antique parchment drum transformed into a coffee table and 19th-century dining table – all pieces he picked up locally.

Throughout, McLachlan used patterned and patinated Portuguese tiles on the floor. “I wanted to add to that potting-shed feel, plus they ground the space and highlight the garden vibe.”

He managed to add a second bedroom, with its own bathroom to boot, into the tiny galley space downstairs. Formerly the photographer’s dark room, it is now a compact guest room, cocooned with the fecund wallpaper and topped off with a small porthole in the bathroom door. “It was just big enough to fit everything in and even my friends who live in big houses love staying down there.”

McLachlan removed the old kitchenette, a small nook that he reinvented as his study, and as a keen musician, it was vital he made space to include an upright piano. Rearranging the kitchen along one wall of the main living space, he utilised the awkward curves and corners in the architecture, replacing them with floor-to-ceiling storage in which to stash his piles of crockery, utensils and linen. Meanwhile, he built a secondary column, emulating an original, whilst adding pleasing symmetry for the eye, but also a useful tool to hide his refrigerator and laundry cupboard.

Another feature is the use of heated skirting boards instead of radiators: “I refused to sacrifice any floor space – even for lovely old cast iron radiators!” he laughs.

McLachlan spent £150,000 on the refit and had builders in for about a year. He believes it has added at least £100,000 in value to the property. “I am all about enhancing the architecture of a particular space and my take on the apartment was informed by that. It seemed an easy decision, particularly as I wanted to create a quiet oasis in this sprawling city. It is also incredibly tranquil, so you really feel like you are stepping in to something very special when you open the door.”

data.title: Burnham’s devolution drive to cost bus operator £260m
data.description:
One of Britain’s biggest bus operators stands to lose £260m from Andy Burnham’s move to hand increased powers to local mayors.

FirstGroup, which runs routes across the UK, said the figure represented lost revenue from services it operates in Wales and Yorkshire that are set to come under municipal control as part of the Prime Minister’s local transport crusade.

The UK is set to move away from privatisation to a bus franchising model whereby local authorities take over fleets and depots and then hire firms to operate them.

Graham Sutherland, FirstGroup’s chief executive, said a franchising model set to be rolled out would deliver lower margins, prompting the group to invest in more dependable markets such as coaches and London buses.

FirstGroup’s switch away from the regions highlights the risks of the Prime Minister’s decision to place buses at the heart of his devolution drive.

It was revealed in August that the West Midlands had been hit with a £30m bill after National Express chose to exit local buses completely in response to franchising, forcing the combined authority to buy out 1,400 vehicles and a network of depots.

FirstGroup’s renewed focus on London comes after it quit the capital in 2013 amid a clampdown by Transport for London (TfL) on the value of contracts.

It reversed the move in December 2024 – less than six months after Labour came to power – with the £90m takeover of RATP London, followed last year by the purchase of the Tootbus sightseeing fleet.

The firm now has more than 1,000 buses in London, with revenue this year expected to rise to £350m, an increase of 13pc.

Mr Sutherland said the franchising of buses in West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire and Wales would deprive FirstGroup of around 30pc of its £890m a year in regional bus revenue.

Industry-wide, he said firms faced a slump of £1.5bn a year in revenue in regions that had already announced their intention to move to franchising.

“We will have materially less regional buses in operation. We’ve diversified on the basis that these policy changes were going to impact our regional bus business,” he said.

“We’re still confident that over the next period of tranches we can continue to grow our bus business.”

FirstGroup said it would monitor plans announced by Lord Khan of Tooting for a new public company – Buses for London – which would compete in the capital, where a franchising model already operates but private firms are allowed to operate their own bus fleets and depots.

Mr Sutherland said: “It’s a handful of routes and a small part of the London network at this point. We don’t think it changes much in the short term and we’re confident that the costs and value we provide will stand up in comparison against any operator.”

Industry sources have called the proposals “mad” and “a Sadiq Khan vanity project” that would heap costs on TfL, which is £14bn in debt.

data.title: Grid under unprecedented pressure as fourth supply warning issued in a week
data.description:
Britain’s grid operator has issued its fourth alert regarding power supplies in a week as the overloaded network struggles to transport electricity from wind farms.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso) issued its latest electricity margin notice on Friday morning, taking the total to 11 so far this year.

This marks a record high, with more notices issued in 2026 than in the previous five years combined.

These alerts reflect a call for extra power supplies and do not signal imminent blackouts. However, the recent surge has renewed fears over Britain’s energy security.

Andrew Larkins, a consultant and former adviser to Neso, said Britain’s energy supplies were facing an “unprecedented situation”.

He told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “The challenge that we have is that we are generating a lot of electricity in the UK and are currently selling quite a lot of that to continental Europe, where there’s a high level of demand.

“But we have a real problem in terms of transporting the electricity generated to where it’s needed.”

Britain’s electricity grid was built primarily in the 1950s, with generators located close to large cities where demand was highest.

But the shift to renewable energy sources means generators are now spread across the country, with major wind farms in Scotland and offshore.

This has resulted in bottlenecks as the ageing grid network struggles to transport supplies to the South. The issue has been compounded by this week’s cold weather, which has driven up demand.

Neso often pays wind farms to switch off when the grid is too congested to carry more power in a practice known as curtailment. The operator must also pay gas-fired power stations in the south to fire up and replace lost supplies.

‘Neso has lost its grip on the grid’

The daily cost of balancing the grid had already hit £47m on Friday morning. Wasted wind has cost the UK more than £2.1bn so far this year, far outstripping the £1.5bn bill racked up in 2025.

Greg Jackson, the chief executive of Octopus Energy, said it was “grotesque” that Britons were being forced to pay vast sums to balance the grid, arguing that “without system reform we are being rinsed”.

Following the latest notice, Kathryn Porter, an independent energy analyst, said: “I think it’s going to be another day of high costs, relying on neighbouring countries and spending a lot on gas power stations because Neso has lost its grip on the grid.”

Ms Porter also criticised Neso for allowing wind farms to sell off power that cannot be used, only to be forced to buy back exports the next day.

She said: “This is expensive and threatens GB energy security if the other countries don’t let us buy them back.”

Neso issues electricity margin notices when its “safety cushion” of emergency power supplies becomes too thin.

The grid operator has blamed this week’s flurry of warnings on engineering work that has further limited the capacity of North-South power lines.

Neso described the warnings as a “routine and precautionary measure, giving market participants the opportunity to make more generation capacity available”.

It added: “This is not a warning of power cuts, there is no risk to customer electricity supplies, and customers do not need to take action.”

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: UK’s biggest gas storage site risks closure after Labour denies support
data.description:
Britain’s biggest gas storage site is in crisis after ministers ruled out providing taxpayer support.

Rough, which is located in the North Sea and operated by British Gas owner Centrica, is at risk of closure within months amid a stand-off over its redevelopment.

Bosses have warned that hundreds of jobs are at risk and are seeking urgent talks with Andy Burnham.

Chris O’Shea, Centrica’s chief executive, told staff on Friday that the company was “doing everything we can to save your jobs”.

In an internal memo, first reported by Sky News, he said: “Frankly, this has taken longer than we expected, given the Government’s stated commitment to reindustrialisation and supporting jobs.

“A decision is now needed, and every month of delay narrows the options available.”

Centrica has been in discussions with ministers about a so-called cap-and-floor mechanism that would help fund a £2bn injection into Rough.

Under this proposal, the company would provide the upfront investment but funding would be effectively guaranteed by a levy on household energy bills.

Labour has yet to make a formal decision on the future of the facility, which represents about half of Britain’s gas storage capacity. But Luke Pollard, the defence minister, rejected calls for government support last month.

Centrica has warned it will not seek a new licence for Rough when the current one expires at the end of April, raising concerns about the future of the site.

Rough supports around 400 jobs, while bosses have argued that the loss-making facility plays a role in national security.

Mr O’Shea has warned Britain is at risk of fuel shortages this winter as gas stockpiles have tumbled, adding that the Iran war energy shock had exacerbated the situation.

Centrica first put forward its proposals for government support a year ago. Mr O’Shea said: “Since then, world events have only made the case for Rough stronger.”

The FTSE 100 utility subsequently raised the idea of using Rough as a strategic gas reserve in the short term.

But Mr O’Shea said Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, had rejected this plan while the Government works through consultation responses.

He said the company wants a “clear signal of where government wants to go on gas storage, how it would support it, and how Rough could keep going in the meantime”.

Centrica said that while no decisions on jobs had been made, it would hold talks with the union, Unite.

A spokesman for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “We have enough gas to meet demand this coming winter – only 5pc of our supply came from storage last winter. 

“We’ve set out plans to maintain our gas security, including options for future commercial support for the sector, while ensuring all proposals provide value for money for consumers.”

data.title: The lesser-known financial benefits of joint accounts
data.description:
Joint bank accounts have traditionally been used by couples to pool their money to pay for household bills and other shared expenses.

However, research by digital wealth manager Moneyfarm shows that almost a third (31pc) of British couples in long-term relationships now refuse to open one at all. Four in 10 view joint accounts as outdated, old-fashioned or even sexist.

Yet despite their declining popularity, joint bank accounts still offer a number of financial benefits – and not just for couples. You can open one with a friend, family member or housemate, too. 

The potential advantages go far beyond making sure you’ve got enough for your next household bill, it could even help out your loved ones after you die.

We’ve spoken to lawyers and tax experts to reveal some of the more surprising financial benefits of opening a joint bank account.

  • Easing probate
  • Inheritance tax advantages
  • Helping to manage finances
  • Advantages for expats
  • What to watch out for

Easing probate

Money held in a joint account automatically passes to the survivor if one of the account holders dies. This can be invaluable if the joint account holder is responsible for covering essential expenses while an estate is going through probate – a process that can take many months. 

During this time, accounts from the deceased will be locked until probate is granted, but with a joint account, the surviving account holder can continue to access joint funds to cover essential expenses.

Duncan Bailey, of law firm Brabners Personal, said: “The surviving partner will need to show a death certificate to the bank to have the account transferred solely into their name. Once this is done, the surviving partner can typically continue using the joint account or regain full access very quickly, without waiting for a grant of probate. This can be a major practical advantage for paying ongoing bills or funeral costs.”

Inheritance tax advantages

For couples who are married or in a civil partnership, transfers between account holders are exempt from inheritance tax.

However, joint accounts aren’t limited to your partner, as you can also open one with a child, other relative, or a friend. In some instances, this arrangement could offer inheritance tax advantages, although it’s not guaranteed and it is essential to seek professional financial advice first.

Mr Bailey said: “Whether inheritance tax applies depends on the specific circumstances, which can sometimes be complex. The crucial factor for inheritance tax purposes is beneficial ownership, which is who actually owns and contributed to the funds in the account.”

One example considered by Mike Warburton, The Telegraph’s tax expert, is whether someone could avoid inheritance tax by opening a joint bank account with their daughter. 

HMRC guidelines suggest that if you simply paid money into this joint account, it would still be “your” money and would form part of your estate on death. But if you did this and made a declaration that the beneficial ownership rests entirely with your daughter, this would count as a lifetime gift to her at that time. 

If you were to survive seven years, the account would fall outside your estate under the seven-year rule. If you died sooner, it may incur a reduced tapered tax rate – assuming it is not covered by the tax-free nil-rate band.

Because the rules are complex, you should keep clear records of all deposits and withdrawals to show who contributed what, in case HMRC makes inquiries later.

Helping to manage finances

Some people use a joint bank account to help manage a relative’s finances, such as paying bills and direct debits, which can be useful when they struggle with online shopping or banking, for example, but still have capacity to be in charge of their own money.

But while this can work informally, it is not a legal substitute for a lasting power of attorney (LPA) should they need something more formal to be set up, warns Stephen Horscroft, of law firm Birketts.

He said: “A bank will typically freeze a joint account if one of the account holders loses capacity. This is because joint accounts rely on the consent of both parties, and the bank has a duty to protect the vulnerable account holder and prevent potential misuse or fraud.

“While essential transactions may still be allowed at the bank’s discretion, non-essential withdrawals are usually blocked until a registered LPA or deputyship order can be provided.”

Advantages for expats

A joint account could also prove useful if you have a friend or relative living overseas who is unable to open a UK account in their sole name because of residency issues.

Mr Horscroft said: “By holding a joint account with a UK-based relative, it can be more straightforward to access UK banking services, pay bills, or receive transfers without the requirement for a UK address.”

However, he also points out that banks may have restrictions on non-resident account holders and anti-money-laundering regulations must still be followed.

What to watch out for

Despite their many advantages, joint accounts come with risks.

Most importantly, you should only ever open a joint account with someone you trust. Each person has equal rights to access and withdraw funds, so if things go wrong, it could be very difficult to recover lost money.

Emma Davies, of law firm Laytons, said: “If either party finds themselves in financial difficulty – for example, bankruptcy or debt – the funds in the joint account will be considered. It is often the case that ownership is presumed to be equal and it can be difficult to prove that this is not the case.

“In this case, it is possible that joint accounts could be frozen temporarily which would limit access to both/all owners – even those who are not involved in the dispute.”

Another important consideration is that opening a joint account creates a financial association on your credit files. If the other person has poor credit, this association could affect your ability to borrow.

Finally, although a joint account can help with access to money after death or incapacity, it shouldn’t replace formal arrangements such as a will or a lasting power of attorney. Always seek professional advice before making significant decisions.

data.title: ‘Ozempic face’ powers revival of a fading British giant
data.description:
A surprise discovery may have saved one of Britain’s oldest chemical companies from sliding into irrelevance.

Croda, founded more than 100 years ago, was once known as the “mini ICI”, a powerhouse industrial giant with 70 factories in Lancashire and Yorkshire.

But like so much of Britain’s chemical industry, its star has been fading in recent years.

A share price rally during Covid – after it teamed up with Pfizer to produce one of the first vaccines – has been fizzling out, with its stock declining for four consecutive years.

Now, however, a surprise discovery is reversing Croda’s fortunes, giving the biotech-to-chemicals group a new lease of life as a beauty giant.

Croda recently discovered that one of its old chemicals can be used to treat “Ozempic face”, the often alarming facial transformation associated with the fat-jab craze.

For about a decade, Croda had been producing a skin-plumping chemical derived from the root of the plant anemarrhena to limited sale success.

Known as Volufiline, the agent swells the skin by chemically expanding fat cells and is used mostly in body creams.

But after users of GLP-1 drugs complained of hollow cheeks and sunken eyes, doctors discovered that Volufiline can combat the gaunt features associated with rapid weight loss.

The discovery has led to an explosion of sales for Croda, turning Volufiline into a TikTok sensation, in demand from the French and South Korean cosmetics industry.

Steve Foots, Croda’s chief executive, said the success of Volufiline had taken everybody by surprise.

“It had been in our portfolio for a decade,” he admits. “Ozempic coming on the market has created a big opportunity, which we’re capitalising on. It can lead to facial hollowing, but we can innovate around that by plumping your skin.”

Revenue from Volufiline sales jumped 270pc in the first half as more than 150 companies signed up to use it in their products.

Videos tagged #Volufiline have also generated 200 million views on the US TikTok Shop app in 12 months.

It has prompted Croda to lean into its new profile as a key force in the burgeoning TikTok influencer economy, helping send shares up 25pc from their August 2025 nadir.

Unlike Botox, Volufiline is applied as a face cream or in a lipstick-style tube.

Estée Lauder, the cosmetics giant, is hooked and has started selling a 92pc concentrate version of Croda’s agent under the Volufiline name.

Croda has even managed to sell it to the Korean “K-beauty” industry, which pioneered the skin-transforming agents and exports $11bn (£8.3bn) every year.

Foots said that while the fat-jabs windfall was unexpected, it had resulted from a decades-long repositioning of Croda from traditional chemicals into a supplier to customers, including L’Oréal, Procter & Gamble and Unilever, as well as Estée Lauder.

Next up is hair care. Alongside Volufiline, Croda is pushing KeraBio, a synthetic form of biotech-derived keratin, as its next miracle product.

While Volufiline was an existing ingredient that found a new use, Foots said KeraBio – developed at Croda’s research facility in Daresbury, Cheshire – will be its “first big product launch in the beauty industry”.

A similar serum from an American rival sells for £80 a shot.

“It’s solving the problem of repairing hair that’s been damaged through combing and heating and colouring, which breaks the keratin bonds,” Foots said.

“It strengthens your hair in a chemical way by creating new bonds, and stops it from ageing, which is a bit of a holy grail in the industry.”

For Croda’s proud British roots, its re-emergence as a cosmetics force is a major boost for the nation’s chemicals sector.

Foots said that while Croda’s business was driven by breakthroughs made at a plant in Daresbury and a second research lab at its headquarters near Goole, East Yorkshire, still not enough was being done to make the UK a chemical powerhouse.

Only 950 of Croda’s 5,500 employees are UK based, and while it has three British plants, most production takes place at factories scattered around Europe, the United States and Asia.

While the beauty industry may be Croda’s new frontier, the firm is also expanding the plant in Leek, Staffordshire, that was so critical in producing lipids used to deliver the Pfizer jab.

A recent breakthrough by Moderna and Merck in developing a melanoma vaccine that uses the same mRNA gene therapy principles shows the potential of the sector, Foots said.

He said: “We were prominent in solving the biggest medical crisis of a generation with the biggest innovation of its time, which was gene therapy drugs. And it’s still advancing.

“Flu vaccines, cancer treatments. The science is there. It will take time to get to market, but we’re excited because Croda is provital in many of these programmes.”

Croda may be one of the few independent British chemicals groups still standing, but its Ozempic discovery proves there’s life in the old dog yet.

data.title: FTSE energy giant quits North Sea over tax raids
data.description:
A British energy giant has quit the North Sea after Labour’s windfall taxes and drilling bans made its operations unviable.

EnQuest, which is listed on the London stock market, said on Wednesday that it had sold its entire UK operation to Neo Next+, a relative newcomer to the North Sea, for a knock-down price of $960m (£730m).

It plans to move its investments to south-east Asia after quitting British waters.

The FTSE 250 company’s UK operations include the giant Magnus and Kraken fields, 1,000 km of key subsea pipelines and the Sullom Voe terminal in Shetland.

EnQuest’s decision follows an industry backlash against John Healey’s decision to keep a windfall tax on North Sea oil and gas profits in place until 2030 despite pressure to scrap it.

Labour’s initial extension of the windfall tax from 2028 to 2030 under Ed Miliband left EnQuest facing a $124m bill, it revealed on Wednesday, pushing the company into a $2m loss for the year.

This was in addition to an $84m bill it paid in 2025, which was much higher than expected after Labour abolished some tax allowances. The windfall tax added another $24m to its tax bill in the first half of this year, alongside $28m in other levies.

Amjad Bseisu, EnQuest’s chief executive, blamed an “uncertain investment environment within the UK”.

The company said it would instead focus on its operations in south-east Asia, aiming to recycle “invested capital from a high-tax, low-return basin into a high-growth region that is structurally short on energy”.

EnQuest’s decision means Neo Next+ will consolidate its position as the North Sea’s largest oil and gas producer.

John Knight, the founder and executive chair of the private equity firm, said: “The addition of EnQuest’s UK oil and gas business further strengthens our scale and resilience in the UK North Sea, while adding production, reserves and cash flow to our portfolio.”

EnQuest is among the UK’s top producers of oil and gas, producing the equivalent of 31,000 barrels of oil a day last year with reserves approaching another 500 million barrels.

Its untapped Bressay and Bentley fields are among the largest in UK waters, capable of producing up to 600 million barrels of oil.

Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said: “The devastating news that EnQuest is withdrawing from the UK is the latest sign that this Government’s policies on oil and gas are hanging a ‘closed for business’ sign over the North Sea.

“We are in the midst of an energy crisis but Labour is still banning licences and maintaining windfall taxes. We need to open the North Sea, abolish the windfall tax and get Britain drilling.”

EnQuest is is the latest energy firm to leave UK waters over Labour’s windfall tax. BP has also announced plans to sell all its UK offshore assets, with the final date for bids due in early December.

Meg O’Neill, BP’s boss, linked the decision to the UK tax regime.

data.title: Amazon to start selling cars in the UK
data.description:
Amazon is to start selling cars in the UK for the first time, marking the expansion of its online car dealership outside the US.

The retail giant will launch Amazon Autos early next year, rolling out a service that will allow customers to select vehicles online before collecting and paying for them at a third-party dealership.

Amazon said the first major car brand to sell its vehicles through the site would be Hyundai, including electric, petrol and hybrid models.

It has also signed up Vertu Motors as the first dealer listing used vehicles on Amazon, with more sellers expected to be announced next year.

Amazon first launched Amazon Autos in the US in 2024, with the service now selling 35 car brands across 150 cities.

Matt Nuffort, director of Amazon Autos International, said: “Buying a car is one of the biggest purchases people make, and we think it should feel as simple and transparent as shopping for anything on Amazon.

“In the UK, that means making it easy for customers to browse available cars, see upfront pricing, reserve the car, and connect with the dealer to finalise the purchase.”

Robert Forrester, the chief executive of Vertu Motors, said Amazon Autos would combine the “convenience and transparency of online shopping with the confidence of completing a purchase through a trusted dealership”.

Amazon’s dealer marketplace will bring it into competition with more established car websites such as Autotrader and used-car app Cinch, which is backed by Asda owner TDR Capital.

Autotrader’s shares fell by more than 3pc in the wake of the announcement, while Vertu was up more than 3.5pc.

An Autotrader spokesman said: “We’ve always welcomed innovation in automotive, but our focus remains on delivering the best possible experience for UK car buyers.”

Amazon’s expansion overseas comes at a time of significant change in the UK and European motor market, as a flurry of new Chinese brands seize share from traditional manufacturers.

BYD, the Chinese electirc vehicle behind the Seal and the Dolphin, has taken close to 6pc of the UK car market, while the Jaecoo 7, made by China’s Chery, emerged as Britain’s top-selling model in September and October.

data.title: EDF acquires UK rival in push to revive prepayment meters
data.description:
EDF has announced a deal to acquire Utilita, strengthening its position in the UK market by taking on the supplier’s 1.3 million customers.

The French state-owned energy firm announced the takeover of Utilita’s parent group, Luxion, on Thursday in a deal set to be completed next year.

EDF accounts for almost 10pc of the UK energy market and serves more than five million homes and businesses.

It is looking to expand further by acquiring Utilita, which was founded in 2003 and specialises in prepayment meters.

More than 90pc of Utilita’s customers use pay-as-you-go meters, which can no longer be forcibly installed after a government crackdown three years ago.

This stemmed from an exposé revealing that agents working for British Gas were breaking into vulnerable customers’ homes to install prepayment meters.

EDF is understood to be preparing for a greater up-tick in prepayment meters as energy bills surge.

Cornwall Insight predicted on Wednesday that the typical household’s annual gas and electricity costs could climb to £2,166 at the start of next year, a £443 increase from the current level.

The deal remains subject to regulatory approval and the two companies will remain independent until that is granted.

Simone Rossi, the chief executive of EDF in the UK, said: “This is a significant step in our ambition to grow EDF’s UK customer business.

“Together, we will have the scale and skills to keep developing services and support for the households who rely on us.”

Bill Bullen, the chief executive of Utilita, said the agreement “builds on an established relationship between the companies, following the successful transfer of 47,000 of Utilita’s residential customers to EDF in November 2025”.

The deal comes amid warnings that Britain’s household energy debt is projected to rise from £5.5bn to £7bn by the end of the year, with at least two million households struggling to keep up with their gas and electricity bills, according to trade body Energy UK.

Some suppliers and analysts have blamed the suspension of forced prepayment meter installations for the recent increase in energy debts.

Prepayment meters automatically disconnect energy supplies unless they are topped up.

Meanwhile, EDF’s proposed acquisition of Utilita comes amid broader consolidation across the UK energy sector.

Eon’s takeover of Ovo Energy was confirmed just last month, adding roughly four million customers to the German energy giant.
