data.title: Norway’s oil and gas supplies to plummet in threat to Britain’s energy
data.description:
Britain faces a massive blow to its energy supplies because of a slump in production in Norway.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday that Norway’s gas production will plummet by one third over the next decade and the Nordic country accounts for 40pc of total UK gas supplies.

Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst at Panmure Liberum, said the coming falls in Norwegian output will be “massively problematic” for the UK and drive up household bills.

Norway also accounts for 69pc of all gas imported into Britain, primarily through pipelines that run across the North Sea.

The IEA’s forecast follows a September report from the Norwegian Offshore Directorate, a government agency that monitors the nation’s reserves, which warned gas production may “fall steeply” from as early as 2030.

This is because new discoveries have not been large enough to maintain current production levels and the output of several major fields will soon decline.

Output at Troll, which is the largest gas field on the Norwegian continental shelf and feeds into the UK’s subsea pipelines, “will plateau rapidly post-2026”, it said.

Mr Kelty warned that the UK will be forced to import more liquefied natural gas (LNG), which is far more expensive.

He said: “The Government seems to think that it is all going to be fine because they’re going to build enough windmills.

“But the grid is not going to be updated quickly enough to compensate for that, so it is just going to mean that the UK has to buy more LNG from the US or Qatar, and that is certainly much more costly.”

LNG is more expensive than pipeline imports because the gas must be compressed and then re-gasified.

The UK and Europe will also be competing with Asian buyers, meaning the region will become even more exposed to global price shocks.

The European Union, which also imports large volumes of gas from Norway, is arguably even more exposed than the UK because it has relatively fewer LNG imports, Mr Kelty said.

The IEA said the decline in Norwegian gas production will be so large that overall gas production in Europe will slump by 13pc by 2035 despite the commissioning of new offshore developments in the Black Sea and Eastern Mediterranean.

Norwegian oil production will also fall by around 30pc by 2035, while the UK’s oil output will sink by 45pc.

Mr Kelty said the numbers highlighted the need for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to give the greenlight for Rosebank in the North Sea.

Mr Kelty said: “It shows that it is absolute lunacy not to develop our own domestic resources. Energy security is key. We have access to oil and gas close to home.”

Mr Burnham signed off on drilling at the Jackdaw gasfield last month, but is yet to announce a decision on Rosebank.

Both fields were given the go-ahead for development under the Conservative government but were then blocked by legal challenges from climate campaign groups.

data.title: Nine steps to protect your money from a cyber attack
data.description:
From high street shops and online marketplaces to supermarket fridges, hackers have exposed how fragile our companies and systems are in a wide-ranging wave of recent cyber attacks.

While much of this is out of your control, you can at least take action to protect your money and personal information – and you don’t have to be particularly tech-savvy to do it.

Kiran Fothergill, of Sapphire Security Services, explained: “Think of it like securing your home. You wouldn’t leave your front door unlocked, hand your keys to a stranger or ignore a broken window. The same common sense should apply online.”

We’ve spoken to cyber security experts to explain the simple steps you can take today to make yourself a harder target for criminals.

1. Lock down your most important accounts

One of the first steps you should take is ensuring your most important accounts are secure.

Zain Javed, of cyber security platform Citation Cyber, said: “If you only make one change today, turn on two-factor authentication, particularly for your email, banking and social media accounts.

“This adds an extra layer of security, so even if a criminal steals your password, they will usually need another form of verification to access your account.”

With two-factor authentication, you’ll usually be asked for a second proof of identity when you sign in, such as a code sent to your phone or generated by an authenticator app.

Free authenticator apps include Duo Mobile, Microsoft Authenticator and Google Authenticator. Where available, using an app rather than receiving codes by text message is generally more secure, as text messages can be intercepted or diverted.

2. Don’t reuse passwords

Remembering umpteen different passwords across various websites isn’t easy. But resist the temptation to use the same password across multiple sites.

Doing so means that if one website has a data breach, criminals could try using your stolen login details to access your other accounts.

Instead, you could use a password manager, such as 1Password or Bitwarden, to generate and securely store unique passwords for different accounts.

Jonathan Lee, of cybersecurity platform TrendAI, said: “Pay particular attention to your personal email account. It can be the front door to much of your digital life, because access to your email may allow someone to reset passwords for other critical services you rely on.”

If passkeys are available on websites, these can be even better than traditional passwords. They let you sign in using your fingerprint, facial recognition or your screen lock PIN.

3. Protect your identity

Your personal information is valuable to criminals, so it’s worth taking steps to protect it.

Mr Fothergill said: “Identity protection services can help you monitor your personal information and identify potential exposure or suspicious activity.

“They aren’t a guarantee against identity theft, but they can provide an additional early warning and help you respond more quickly.”

However, you might not need to pay for a specialist service.

Paul Bischoff, of research company Comparitech, said: “Identity protection apps don’t do much that you can’t do yourself, such as monitoring bank accounts and credit. For most of us, these apps are mainly a convenience.”

Instead, you can take some simple steps such as regularly checking your bank and credit card statements for unfamiliar transactions, checking your free credit report for accounts you don’t recognise, and being alert to unexpected password reset emails.

4. Don’t give personal details to AI

With increasing numbers of people turning to AI to ask for advice on everything from medical issues to personal finance, you need to think carefully about the information you share.

Tom Vazdar, of Open Institute of Technology, said: “Treat an AI chatbot like a stranger with a very good memory. Conversations may be stored, read by reviewers or leaked. Don’t type in passwords, bank details, ID documents, medical records or work files.”

Also check your provider’s privacy settings as not all AI platforms handle data in the same way.

Charles Radclyffe, of EA Global AI, said: “Consumer AI tools may use user interactions to help improve and train their models, so users should think carefully before sharing personal information.”

5. Don’t ignore app and device updates

Another simple but important step is to ensure you have turned on automatic updates on your phone, laptop, web browser and apps. It can pay to keep the built-in security features on your devices switched on, too.

Mr Javed said: “Those software update notifications we all put off are actually one of the simplest ways to protect ourselves.

“Cybercriminals regularly exploit known weaknesses in outdated software. Manufacturers release updates to fix these vulnerabilities, but those fixes only protect you once they’re installed.”

6. Guard your bank account

Scammers are finding ever more convincing ways to part people from their cash, which makes it even more important to be on your guard.

Mr Javed said: “The days of spotting a scam because of poor spelling or bad grammar are disappearing. AI means criminals can now write convincing messages and even imitate familiar voices.”

To protect yourself, agree a family code word and ask for it if someone calls asking for money.

Mr Fothergill added: “Criminals are very good at creating a sense of urgency. You might receive a text claiming there’s suspicious activity on your bank account or a telephone call warning that your money is at risk. The golden rule is never to act under pressure.”

This means never clicking on links in unexpected messages or sharing passwords, Pins or security codes with someone who contacts you. If you’re unsure, always hang up and contact your bank directly using the number on the website or through the official app.

Remember, your bank will never ask for your Pin or account details or request you transfer money into a so-called “safe account”.

7. Stick to familiar websites

When shopping online, stick to trusted websites you’ve used before. Criminals can create convincing copies of genuine websites, so check the web address carefully before entering any personal or payment details.

Even if the website has a padlock symbol or “https” address, this doesn’t mean the website is safe.

You should also be wary of adverts and offers that seem too good to be true.

Jamie Akhtar, of cybersecurity platform CyberSmart, said: “Cybercriminals are quick to exploit trending topics, using the excitement surrounding popular games, new film releases and other cultural moments to trick unsuspecting users into clicking malicious links or downloading harmful content.

“If you receive a message promising exclusive access, early releases or special offers, take a moment to verify that it comes from a legitimate source before clicking any links or sharing personal information.”

8. Delete apps you don’t use

Most of us have far too many apps on our phones, so it’s worth having a digital clear out every so often.

The more apps and services you give access to your personal information, the more potential ways there are for it to be exposed if an account or company is compromised.

Art Gilliland, of cyber firm Delinea, said: “Check which apps you’ve allowed to read your emails, see your contacts or access your files. Remove connections you no longer use. Don’t forget that deleting an app from your phone doesn’t necessarily cancel its access.”

It’s also worth reviewing the permissions of the apps you keep and switching off access to your camera, microphone, location or contacts if they don’t need it.

9. Regularly back-up files

Finally, don’t forget to back-up files on your phone or laptop. Doing this means you’ll still have access to important information if your device is damaged, lost or compromised in a cyber attack.

You can do this using a trusted cloud service or an external drive that isn’t permanently connected to your computer.

Mr Fothergill said: “Cyber attacks aren’t always about stealing money. Ransomware and malicious software can also lock you out of family photographs, important documents and personal records.”

Try to back-up your files regularly and check you can restore them if needed.

data.title: The 33-year-old at the forefront of Britain’s defence revolution
data.description:
To see the future of Britain’s defence industry, you have to visit a four-storey building found on what used to be a car park off Old Kent Road. This clean and functional edifice is the biggest new factory in London since the Second World War.

A Union Flag overlooks the factory floor, where 12 machines are silently engaged in turning steel, aluminium and titanium into precision components for jet engines, drones, robots and much more.

Presiding over them is Alexander Fitzgerald, the 33-year-old founder and chief executive of the company, Isembard, which he established in late 2024.

Like everyone who creates a successful business, the T-shirt-wearing entrepreneur spotted a problem and proposed a solution. “What’s happening across every single sector right now – from aerospace to defence to robotics to energy to semiconductors – is that demand is massively increasing, but the supply of manufacturing capacity to make those components is reducing,” he says.

Isembard’s driving purpose is to provide some of that desperately needed extra capacity. The opportunity is all the greater because of a revolution sweeping Britain’s defence industry.

For generations, the sector has been dominated by a handful of large “prime contractors”, such as BAE Systems, which specialise in the slow and hugely expensive production of a relative handful of advanced jet fighters, tanks and warships, designed to stay in service for decades.

But the lesson from Ukraine is that there are increasing – and critical – advantages for countries that can speedily produce an abundance of smaller and cheaper systems, such as drones, then constantly improve and redesign them, and turn out new and better models every few months. This requires a multitude of small and medium-sized enterprises that can compete to be the most innovative and efficient by deploying AI to make an ever-changing array of components as quickly and cheaply as possible.

Isembard is already doing exactly that. Companies send 3D designs for the parts they need, and Isembard manufactures them according to those designs. “We build our own software and AI to make setting up our factories and running our factories really efficient,” says Fitzgerald.

At present, about 95 per cent of components for manufacturing are produced by small and medium-scale businesses. It is an extraordinary fact that the average age of the owners of these companies in the UK is 65 – and that no less than 40 per cent of them plan to retire within five years.

At the exact moment when Europe is rearming – with all Nato countries, including Britain, pledging to spend at least 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035 – the supply chain for new components is contracting.

Hence, Isembard is expanding rapidly to meet pent-up demand. Fitzgerald opened his first factory last year, and today his company has 18 worldwide – eight in Britain, eight in America and one each in France and Germany.

This growth has been accelerated by Isembard’s unique business model, which allows for franchised factories. All but five of the existing plants are not owned by the company, but franchised to individual operators. The newest, in Swindon, took a mere 90 days to set up, and Fitzgerald aims to get this down to one or two weeks.

Speed and agility are everything. Fitzgerald notes that what has allowed Ukraine to resist the Russian invaders is not one kind of exquisitely engineered drone, but rather a vast and constantly changing array of different models. “In Ukraine, it’s not one type of drone – and 10 billion of them,” he says. “It’s a zoo of different types of drones, at all classes and all stages. Then you need to be able to scale up.”

Fitzgerald adds: “You need a manufacturing base, which is fundamentally a question of, ‘Have you got enough stuff that can make stuff? Have you networked them enough to be more efficient?’ That’s really the core of our business.”

Reindustrialising Britain by reshoring production is, he believes, the key to the country’s future prosperity. “The grand theory of everything is manufacturing because it’s the root of our prosperity, security and purpose,” he says. “I subscribe to the manufacturing dream – that means security and prosperity [depend on] your ability to make stuff.”

Nearby, the computer numerical control (CNC) machines – which have affectionate nicknames such as Cathy and Big Bertha – on the factory floor are playing their part in reindustrialising Britain by turning out the precisely shaped objects that will soon be flying at high speed as the components of jet engines or drones.

The factory, which covers three floors and 160,000 square feet, aims to triple its workforce to 200 by the end of next year. Taking delivery of the hulking CNCs required Fitzgerald to install a bigger loading door in the building, which was previously used as a grocery depot. The machines had to arrive in the early hours of the morning, since there are timing restrictions within three miles of Charing Cross for loads of that weight and size.

Fitzgerald emphasises that Isembard is not a “defence tech company”, but rather a “manufacturing company”. About 60 per cent of its customers are in aerospace and defence, while most of the rest are in robotics.

But Russia is unlikely to be interested in that distinction as its intelligence services carry out their escalating campaign of sabotage and subversion across Europe, including in Britain.

Is Fitzgerald concerned about that threat? “Yes, and I think the Government should be concerned,” he replies. “We have good security protections in both the cyber and the physical side. We’ve had a lot of support from the Government, and from the police and other agencies, as well.”

Fitzgerald has personal experience of Whitehall, since he spent three years as a Treasury civil servant after graduating from Nottingham University with a degree in biochemistry. Earlier, he had also tried his hand at journalism as an intern at City AM.

He enjoyed his time working in the Government, but cannot help remembering: “When I thought I had the right answer for something, it still had to go through six pairs of hands to get to someone to make a decision. That frustrated me.”

He left the Treasury to start a broadband company that amassed almost 100,000 customers before he sold it to Octopus Group in 2022. Fitzgerald founded Isembard soon afterwards, and the company now makes components for customers like Anduril, which manufactures drones and autonomous weaponry, and Oxford Space Systems, which produces the antennae for satellites.

In the past, certain British investors and banks had a fastidious disdain for any businesses linked to defence, some of which were denied financial services. Fitzgerald, who is also an Army reservist, has encountered no such difficulties, and he believes that attitudes have changed. “I think Ukraine has changed that,” he says. “Geopolitics has changed that.”

Something else that has changed is the attitude towards manufacturing in general. One of Andy Burnham’s central priorities is “reindustrialisation” and recapturing the dynamism of former years.

In that spirit, Fitzgerald named his company after the great Victorian engineer, Isambard Kingdom Brunel, though he adapted the spelling of his hero’s Christian name because the original domain had already been taken.

Today, he keeps a black top hat on his desk in tribute to the man whose individual drive and genius powered Britain’s first industrial revolution.

His other inspiration is Lord Beaverbrook, the minister for aircraft production in 1940, who galvanised British industry into delivering 100 Spitfires and Hurricanes every week, making him an architect of victory in the Battle of Britain and changing the course of the Second World War.

“The Air Ministry didn’t like him. He was threatening to resign the whole time, but he got the job done,” says Fitzgerald, who notes that Beaverbrook tripled production in a matter of months by distributing the manufacture of Spitfire and Hurricane components between hundreds of superbly innovative and cost-efficient small and medium enterprises across the country.

That formula saved Britain in 1940. It might yet do the same again.

data.title: Elon Musk to kill off Tesla’s Cybertruck
data.description:
Elon Musk is to end production of Tesla’s Cybertruck after sales of the controversial electric pick-up proved a disappointment.

The electric carmaker’s chief executive signalled last night that production of the Cybertruck will wind down in 2027, making way for the business to produce more robotaxis at its Texas Gigafactory.

Posting on social media, Mr Musk said: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

The announcement comes just three years after the Cybertruck first went on sale.

Mr Musk had hailed the three-ton vehicle as “bulletproof” and “apocalypse-proof”, while the company’s website promotes its “ultra-hard stainless-steel exoskeleton” and a range of up to 325 miles.

However, the truck’s high price dampened demand among motorists.

It was initially set to cost $39,999 (£30,600) but the cheapest version now starts at $60,000 (£45,900).

Tesla sold just 11,586 Cybertrucks in the first nine months of 2026, according to analysts Cox Automotive, far below Mr Musk’s previous predictions of 250,000 sales a year.

While Mr Musk had billed the pick-up as the ultimate off-road electric vehicle, the Cybertruck has suffered from a series of mishaps and faults before and after it went on sale.

When demonstrating the truck’s toughened glass during its 2019 launch event, a Tesla executive threw a ball bearing at its window, causing it to shatter.

Tesla has also been forced to issue recalls of the truck over braking issues and other problems, including the vehicle’s trim falling off.

Several trucks have been involved in accidents where they have burst into fireballs after a crash.

Mr Musk took the decision to end production as he attempts to revive Tesla by focusing on AI, robotics and driverless taxis, increasing production of its Cybercab vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots.

The company has launched ride-hailing services in a handful of US cities, while it is planning to build up to 125,000 autonomous electric cabs per year at its flagship Texas plant.

Shares in Mr Musk’s companies have plunged this week after the Democrats swung to victory in the US midterm elections, taking both the House and the Senate.

Tesla’s stock is down more than 12pc since Tuesday, while SpaceX is down 11pc. Mr Musk’s net worth plummeted by close to $80bn in one day on Thursday to around $785bn, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index.

data.title: BBC calls in restructuring experts to accelerate cost-cutting drive
data.description:
The BBC has turned to restructuring experts at AlixPartners as Matt Brittin, the director-general, steps up efforts to strip £500m of costs from the embattled broadcaster.

The consultancy firm, which specialises in turnaround plans for distressed companies, has been tapped to help the BBC find further savings after repeated rounds of gruelling cuts.

Advisers are understood to have been tasked with accelerating existing cost-cutting measures by focusing on “three Ps” – people, procurement and programming.

This means they will seek out further savings through job reductions, cuts to shows and channels, and reviewing how much the broadcaster spends on suppliers.

The move comes despite BBC bosses pledging earlier this year to reduce costs spent on management consultants.

Rhodri Talfan Davies, the deputy director-general, said in April that reducing the broadcaster’s £5m annual bill on external advisers would make a “meaningful contribution” to its broader cost-cutting push.

The BBC declined to comment on how much it was paying AlixPartners for its services. The New York-headquartered consultancy charges an hourly rate of up to $1,500 (£1,150).

A spokesman said the savings achieved would significantly outweigh the costs, adding that the corporation was focused on protecting investment in its output for audiences.

Wielding the axe

New York-based AlixPartners, which was founded in 1981, is known for its interventions in high-stakes corporate turnarounds and insolvencies.

The consultancy has advised on some of the largest US bankruptcies, including General Motors and Enron, while it helped identify thousands of victims of Bernie Madoff’s multibillion-dollar Ponzi scheme.

More recently, AlixPartners was appointed joint administrator of collapsed shadow bank Market Financial Solutions (MFS) and has been lined up for a potential Poundland collapse.

AlixPartners also acted as the receiver of the titles of The Telegraph after they were seized from the Barclay family by Lloyds Bank in June 2023.

The appointment suggests a change of tack by Mr Brittin, the former Google executive who took the helm at the BBC in May.

The public service broadcaster has outlined plans to cut around 1,800 jobs – or 11pc of its workforce – over the next three years as part of its efforts to save £500m.

It follows a previous £700m cost-cutting programme, which was launched in 2022 and focused on productivity improvements.

However, the public spending watchdog last week warned that the BBC would struggle to find further savings without harming audiences.

The corporation has wielded the axe on programmes including Celebrity Mastermind, Live at the Apollo and Radio 4’s The World Tonight, while it is closing entire channels such as BBC Three and BBC Scotland.

A BBC spokesman said: “Due to the significant financial challenge we face, the BBC needs to deliver an additional £500m of savings over the next three years.

“While substantial work has already been undertaken internally, external expertise can help us identify and deliver sustainable savings more quickly across a large and complex organisation.”

AlixPartners declined to comment.

data.title: Ofgem launches urgent inquiry into power grid delays
data.description:
Britain’s energy watchdog has launched an urgent inquiry into plans to accelerate electricity grid connections after they inadvertently caused more delays.

Ofgem said on Thursday it would investigate why an overhaul designed to speed up access to the grid had instead made it harder to secure a connection.

Developers have complained about lengthy waits to have their sites hooked up to electricity, which has stalled the rollout of new factories and homes.

The regulator said it shared the “frustration” of developers, acknowledging the outcomes from its reforms were “not good enough”.

The National Energy System Operator had been tasked with weeding out so-called “zombie projects” from a queue of schemes waiting for a connection.

However, Ofgem said that “the majority of projects in the reformed queue are seeing delays rather than advancements”.

Akshay Kaul, the energy watchdog’s director-general for infrastructure, said that the connection dates offered to too many projects were “not good enough”.

“Our inquiry will establish transparently what has driven these delays,” he said.

The inquiry came as Labour moved to scrub all mention of its controversial 2030 green energy policy from an announcement hailing the latest round of net zero subsidies.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero on Thursday appeared to distance itself further from a target to run the UK’s electricity grid entirely on low-carbon technologies by the end of the decade.

Known as Clean Power 2030, the proposal was a centrepiece of Labour’s election manifesto and championed by Ed Miliband, who became energy secretary.

However, the policy appears to have been dropped from government communications after an announcement on new wind and solar farm subsidies omitted the reference.

It comes after Mr Miliband was moved to the Foreign Office this summer, replaced by Miatta Fahnbulleh as Energy Secretary.

His departure was quickly followed by that of Chris Stark, appointed by Mr Miliband to oversee the Clean Power 2030 programme.

Ministers still refer to “clean power”, but they set no date and are pledging to reform the system to focus on costs rather than timelines.

It follows warnings from John Healey, the Chancellor, that while he supported clean power “we will only buy projects that can lower bills while strengthening our energy security”.

Michael Shanks, the energy minister, has also said future clean power projects had to prioritise lower bills.

“These reforms … make the auction process more transparent and competitive, so we secure the best projects at the best price for consumers,” he said.

The shift in emphasis from decarbonisation by 2030 to cutting prices is likely to mean fewer applications or approvals for new renewables projects.

These have always been heavily reliant on subsidies in the form of Contracts for Difference.

However, the latest auction round set no effective budget for the subsidies, leaving developers uncertain of the funding.

data.title: ‘Tesla of China’ could make cars in Britain as Burnham considers tariffs
data.description:
A company nicknamed the “Tesla of China” is considering manufacturing its vehicles in Britain as Andy Burnham mulls tariffs on Beijing’s electric car companies.

Brian Gu, the vice-chairman and president of Xpeng, told The Telegraph it would be “natural to think about local manufacturing” if sales in Britain hit a certain level.

The comments came as the Guangzhou-headquartered company this week announced plans to launch five new luxury vehicles aimed at British buyers.

Xpeng has been seen as a potential challenger to Tesla, pursuing a similar strategy of hi-tech vehicles packed with self-driving technology, while it has also developed humanoid robots.

Its sleek coupes, such as the LO3, share similarities with Tesla’s vehicles, pitting the Chinese companies directly against Elon Musk’s car business.

At a launch at the luxury Fairmont Windsor Park Hotel on Thursday, Xpeng unveiled the UK version of its LO3 SUV coupe, which it said would start at £32,990 and feature a range of more than 300 miles.

Speaking to The Telegraph, Mr Gu said the company would consider building vehicles in Britain if its launch in the market is a success.

Mr Gu said: “It depends on the success that we anticipate from these launches. We hope to generate a substantial business. And once we reach a certain volume, then it’s natural to think about local manufacturing.”

It comes as the Prime Minister considers imposing tariffs on Chinese electric cars. The EU has already enforced steep tariffs of up to 35.3pc on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) and the Prime Minister has been seeking closer ties with Europe, raising the prospect the UK will adopt similar rules.

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, has been drafting a tariff blueprint and Anas Sarwar, the trade minister, said last month that Britain and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to combat the flood of Chinese EV imports.

Xpeng’s latest UK vehicles will be built in China and shipped to Britain, meaning they would fall foul of any prospective tariff regime. It also produces cars for Europe out of a factory in Austria, although this plant is already near full capacity.

Xpeng’s launch in Britain follows a flood of other Chinese car brands that have swept across the UK market. The Jaecoo 7, made by China’s Chery, was the UK’s top-selling car in September, while BYD, which makes electric cars such as the Seal, has claimed close to 10pc of EV and hybrid sales so far this year.

The European tariffs have prompted Chinese carmakers to shift more production into the bloc to avoid the levies.

Some are also now exploring similar arrangements in the UK in anticipation of potential tariffs here. Chery, whose Jaecoo 7 is known as the “Temu Range Rover” for its lookalike appearance of the British marque, has sealed a deal with Nissan to explore making its cars in Sunderland.

Mr Gu said Chery’s deal was “very much a validation of their success in the UK market”. “If you want to be a leading player, you have to have more local capabilities,” he said.

The Xpeng boss said the company would have to “react” to any new UK rules on Chinese imports. It previously began making cars with Austrian manufacturer Magna in 2025 after Europe brought in its own tough levies.

Mr Gu said: “We have to react to whatever arrangement or regime there is, just like when we reacted to Europe when they announced EV tariffs on Chinese brands.

“We want to keep the current open, friendly and conductive market environment. But we as a company need to react whenever there is change.”

Xpeng plans to build a network of 100 retail outlets and service stations across the UK by the end of 2027. It is planning to open three flagship stores in London and Manchester in the next six months.

The company also announced plans to explore bringing its robotaxi service, known as Yoyo, to UK roads. “London is a very important, key robotaxi market. We also want to see how Yoyo can be tested,” Mr Gu said.

data.title: Grid operator issues third warning this week over power shortages
data.description:
Britain’s grid operator has issued its third warning regarding power supplies this week as concerns grow surrounding the effect of wasted wind.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso) issued electricity margin notices (EMNs) for Thursday – the third alert this week – as network bottlenecks forced it to replace wind power that could not be transported.

Neso insisted the latest warning was “routine and precautionary” and did not signal imminent power cuts.

However, the alert has renewed scrutiny of the UK’s energy supplies as it becomes increasingly reliant on intermittent renewables.

The latest scramble is expected to result in a flurry of expensive and last-minute trades for replacement power that will end up costing billpayers millions of pounds.

It comes after Neso was forced to buy back large amounts of power at a premium earlier this week after issuing two previous shortfall warnings.

Kathryn Porter, an independent energy analyst, accused the grid operator of standing by while wind farms in Scotland sold power that could not be used, as planned maintenance work squeezes the capacity of power lines.

The cost of balancing actions rose above £55m on Thursday afternoon, according to a tracker website, marking a fresh record. The total costs related to wasted wind have exceeded £2bn so far in 2026.

Ms Porter said: “Neso has to curtail this wind but then the market is short once it’s taken away.

“So Neso has to bring up gas plant in the balancing mechanism and buy back the exports. It could curtail this wind the day before delivery, to stop the market behaving as if it’s real, but for some reason it doesn’t.

“So regularly now we see Neso doing expensive last-minute balancing actions instead of planning ahead properly.”

Wind farms in Scotland and the North are often paid to switch off – a practice known as curtailment – when the grid is too congested to carry their power further south.

When this happens, Neso is typically forced to replace the electricity with power generated by gas-fired plants.

However, curtailment does not usually lead to EMNs being issued on its own.

As part of its job keeping Britain’s lights on, Neso must keep a “safety cushion” of spare power available for emergencies.

When this cushion becomes too small – usually because national electricity supplies have grown tighter – the grid operator can issue EMNs to ask power stations to make any spare capacity they have available.

Neso faces fresh scrutiny

Neso said this week’s warnings were the result of “significant constraints on the network caused by maintenance and reinforcement work by transmission owners” – a reference to engineering work being done that has throttled the capacity of north-south power lines.

Originally issued as a single alert, the first of Thursday’s notices now covers the six-hour period from 8am to midday while the other covers midday to 8pm.

This week’s EMNs have prompted fresh scrutiny of the grid balancing system and whether it is good value for money.

The UK has some of the highest balancing costs in Europe. Neso said last week it had sought a £1bn loan from the Treasury to meet soaring wasted wind payments, which are ultimately passed on to consumers.

Ms Porter said she expected Neso would try to curb electricity exports to the Continent to help address Thursday’s safety cushion shortfall.

But she added: “The big question is whether [neighbouring European countries] will let Neso keep buying all day.”

If not, she warned, Neso could be forced to issue “emergency instructions” to reduce exports to the Continent, or impose “demand reduction” measures such as voltage curbs and controlled power cuts.

She called on the regulator Ofgem and the Government to “get a grip on this and force Neso to start balancing earlier, so phantom wind isn’t creating these problem exports in the first place”.

“It’s not just expensive, it also risks GB energy security,” she added.

A Neso spokesman said: “We have issued an EMN for Nov 26 as a routine and precautionary measure, giving market participants the opportunity to make additional generation capacity available.

“This is not a warning of power cuts, there is no risk to customer electricity supplies, and customers do not need to take action.”

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Housebuilder’s shares collapse as property slowdown crushes profits
data.description:
Shares in Crest Nicholson plunged by as much as 30pc on Monday after it warned of deepening losses caused by Britain’s property slowdown.

The developer said it was now forecasting losses of between £30m and £40m for the year to the end of October, significantly worse than the £10m loss it had predicted in September.

Crest Nicholson has repeatedly downgraded its guidance this year as it becomes the latest housebuilder to struggle amid economic turmoil unleashed by the Iran war.

Demand has been dampened after the conflict pushed up both mortgage rates and energy costs.

The company said that it had completed 1,353 homes in the 12 months to the end of October, at the bottom end of its guidance of between 1,350 and 1,400, which it had cut from 1,500 earlier this year.

It comes after a string of property developers have already warned that rising costs and regulations are making new house-building projects challenging.

Crest Nicholson’s shares are at a record low, as investors turn away from Britain’s housebuilding sector.

Rival developers were also down on Monday in the wake of Crest Nicholson’s update. Vistry sank by 2.6pc, Barratt Redrow lost 1.3pc and Taylor Wimpey was also down 1.2pc.

In an update to investors, Crest Nicholson said: “Trading conditions deteriorated further through the group’s fourth quarter, reflecting continued weak demand across the sector, driven by the uncertain geopolitical and macro environment.”

The London-listed company added that it “expects the current challenging trading conditions to persist well into next year”.

The housebuilder also said it is “reviewing the profitability of sites” because of a triple whammy of poor sales, weak pricing and persistent inflationary pressures on the cost of building materials.

A series of property developers have warned that cost pressures, regulation and weak demand have made housebuilding unviable in recent months.

Jennie Daly, the boss of housebuilder Taylor Wimpey, warned last month that building in London was “fundamentally broken”, and that the incentive to take on risky projects had “evaporated”.

While figures released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) last year showed that home completions across England dropped to their lowest level since 2016.

data.title: Confessions of the middle-class money savers
data.description:
This week, millions of shoppers will be waiting in anticipation, clicking-fingers a-quiver, for the bells of Black Friday and Cyber Monday to peal. This curious retail extravaganza might have begun as an American phenomenon tied to the Thanksgiving holiday, but it has long since spread globally. Love it or loathe it, it has established itself, knotweed-like, in the British retail calendar. Research commissioned by PayPal estimates that this year British shoppers will spend £6.7bn across the two days, up £700m on last year.

In recent years, against a backdrop of rising prices, particularly for energy, the timeless hunt for a bargain has coincided with seemingly endless reasons to be thrifty. A new study by the British Retail Consortium (BRC) has found that with household costs continuing to rise, waiting for a good deal on Black Friday has been one reason British shoppers have been holding back in recent months.

“During the cost of living crisis, people are having to be more savvy about finding ways to save money,” says Tom Holder, a BRC spokesman. “They feel like they’ve got less money in their pocket once all the bills and energy costs have been paid. Even middle-class families have been turning to basic ranges in supermarkets. Between the internet and the rise of AI, there are ever more opportunities for people to try to dig out deals. People are willing to wait for prices to drop.” An increasing risk surrounding Black Friday, he adds, is that it ends up diluting spending. Retailers are increasingly wary of offering deep discounts to customers who have shown they are more than willing to wait and pounce.

French revolutionaries might have disparagingly called Britain a nation of shopkeepers, but we are equally a nation of bargain-hunters, vigilant for opportunities to save a few quid wherever possible. If there was ever a stigma surrounding thrift, it looks quaintly old-fashioned today. Nobody is immune. In 2011, Benedict Cumberbatch asked an interviewer whether they ought to share a teabag (Earl Grey). He shares this trait with Rod Stewart.

“I think a love of a bargain is part of British culture,” says Holly Jay-Smith, a money-saving influencer known as the Coupon Queen, who has more than half a million followers on TikTok. “If someone compliments us on something we’re wearing, we can’t wait to tell them where we got it and how much we paid for it. There’s a real sense of satisfaction in knowing you’ve got something for a fraction of its original price, regardless of how much money you have. I also think the stigma around shopping in bargain stores and buying reduced products has disappeared. People are proud to share how much they’ve saved.”

While this week the spotlight might be on retail, the quest for value has strengthened across the board. Here we have identified five archetypes. Whether you prefer easyJet over private planes, are willing to drive out of your way for cheaper petrol, avoid branded paracetamol, or set your dishwasher to run in the middle of the night, you can be sure you are among friends. There is a reason Martin Lewis, the Money Saving Expert, is routinely ranked as a dream prime minister, just behind David Attenborough. There is only one thing Britons love as much as animals – and that’s a bargain.

Travel scrimpers

Travel might broaden the mind, but it can tighten the purse strings, too. I like to think I am reasonably generous in other areas of my life. I get a round in. I don’t mind if the central heating goes on. (That’s what it’s for!) I am not averse to minor fripperies. But there is something about the prospect of paying extra for luggage that turns me into Scrooge McDuck. Where other travellers hate airlines such as Ryanair and easyJet for restricting luggage, I see it as a delightful challenge. I personally insist on travelling as light as possible: underseat hand luggage only, regardless of the duration or type of trip.

I recently interviewed Michael O’Leary, the Ryanair boss. He made the point that when passengers complain that he wants too much of their money, they have it backwards; the airline simply does not want your luggage. I empathise.

But my obsessive luggage-avoidance pales in comparison with some money-saving quests. In 2016, 18-year-old Jordon Cox made headlines when he flew from Sheffield to Essex via Berlin, rather than take the train, saving himself £7.72.

I asked for contributions on social media, and it turned up some more egregious examples. “A guy I knew was offered a spot in a private jet,” writes one respondent. “But when he found out the taxi fare to the airfield was marginally more than a Ryanair flight, he just took the Ryanair flight.”

Cars can be occasions for economising, too. “As a legacy of my father’s petrol-price obsession, I will drive 10 miles or more out of my way to find the cheapest filling station,” writes reader Nina Dempsey. “It’s ridiculous, since the maximum I ever save is about £1.70, which is spent on an overpriced chocolate bar on the same visit.”

Cyber sleuths

Technology, particularly the internet, has long been a boon to bargain hunters, who can sit there waiting for just the right discount. But it’s getting harder to find a good deal. This week, a Which? investigation of more than 250,000 prices found that only 22 per cent of the offers were cheaper during the four-week Black Friday sales period last year than at any other point in the year.

Still, Black Friday or not, some shoppers will never stop using the internet to hunt for discounts, even if the value is not obvious. “I’ll only buy clothes if I get a discount code,” writes one friend. “I don’t mean cheap clothes, either. I’ll spend £1,200 on a second-hand Gucci Blinde bag from FarFetch or a ridiculous cashmere coat from Net-a-Porter, but only if I’ve got a ‘first-time customer 10 per cent off’ code. Hence I have about 10,000 email addresses.”

For shoppers, it is not the discount itself that causes pain, but the shipping. “I will inconvenience myself and travel to Kent for ‘free collection’ to save the £6.99,” writes one correspondent who lives in Tufnell Park, north London. “It’s a way to get back at Evri.”

Apart from emails, the more tech-savvy will now have AI agents working day and night to hunt out value across the internet. Black Friday and Cyber Monday might be once a year, but every Friday is Black and every Monday is Cyber to people who know what they are doing.

Faithful thrifters

Where once there might have been a mild stigma around buying from charity shops, it has long since vanished. According to Robin Osterley, the chief executive of the Charity Retail Association, two factors have helped remove any lingering middle-class reluctance to use charity shops: sustainability and the rise of online second-hand platforms such as Vinted.

“It is almost reversing,” he says of the shopping trends. “My son is 24. A few years ago, he wouldn’t have been seen dead in a charity shop. But with him and his mates starting to buy stuff on Vinted, it is becoming quite cool. The zeitgeist has changed among Gen Z. People understand that we are manufacturing far too much stuff, importing almost-disposable clothing from the Far East.”

Restaurants, too, are one area where thrift has become surprisingly common. “My 73-year-old father pre-loads on bread before going out to a restaurant for lunch,” writes one reader. “Then he only orders a tiny thing, like a side of olives, while everyone else gets a normal lunch. So embarrassing, such bad manners, so overtly cheap.” Another says she has “never once bought tissues – I will only use Pret napkins, or kitchen roll”, while another respondent admits to having “stolen loo roll from pubs”.

Another man tells me that “a family member weighs their salmon on the supermarket fruit and veg scales, as even though packets are all listed as being the same weight, he has realised that there are discrepancies”. Even in the kitchen, that is no time to slack off on the quest for value. “I constantly reuse and bits of foil and cling film because they fit neatest on to bowls and jars,” writes one man. “We have a corner of the kitchen overflowing with different-sized scraps.”

There are opportunities in every café for those with the right mindset. “My mother doesn’t have sugar in her tea or coffee, but sees the sugar sachets as part of purchase – so in the handbag they go,” one woman tells me. “Same with the biscuit, ketchup, mayo, mints, hotel toiletries and any other such items. As a child, I once managed to make a cake with 200g of sugar from those little sachets. Mum was very proud.”

Martin Lewis disciples

The true believers are the devoted congregation of the Money Saving god. “Would you throw that cash in the bin?” they ask. “No. So why would you not switch energy providers nine times a year? Or car insurance, or mobile phone company, or any of the other thousand demands on your direct debit?” Life is too short for this stuff, you reply. They disagree.

Martin Lewis’s website is full of testimonials from the ordinary Britons whose lives he has made just that little bit more economical: Maureen, who haggled her Sky broadband and TV bill down from £83 per month to £39. Alex Motley, who saved £1,200 on council tax and £9,000 for his neighbours thanks to Lewis’s tips. “My whole shtick is to maximise happiness with your money,” Lewis has said. No wonder the country would love to see him in No 10.

Among the Lewis disciples is Mick Wall, who was inspired to create his own site, energy-stats.uk, dedicated to energy saving. Wall says that insulation is the simplest way for most people to save money, but that you can also make your heating more efficient by running a gas boiler lower. Oh, and an electric car. “When there’s £2 diesel or £1.70 petrol, an electric car is way cheaper to run. But the problem with all this stuff – heat pumps, solar batteries, EVs – is that there is a capital cost you have to find in the first place. It is almost like a middle-class subsidy.” That’s the irony of energy saving: it helps to have money in the first place.

The variable tariffs in off-peak times are irresistible to the energy bargain hunter. “I obsessively set the dishwasher and the washing machine to run only between 11.30pm and 5.30am, to make the most of our energy tariff,” one friend tells me. “I think it saves around 7p.”

Point savers

It is possible to remember a time when one could complete a transaction in Britain without accruing points or loyalty of some kind, but only just. Today at every supermarket till, Boots and most restaurants, you will be asked not only for your money but your membership of the relevant club, as well: Nectar, Advantage, ClubCard, Sparks, MyWaitrose.

Systems have given rise to people who will look to maximise or even exploit them, which can lead to some unusual behaviour. This is an ancient art: it was nearly 30 years ago that Phil Calcott, a Worcester physicist, worked out a loophole in the Tesco Clubcard scheme whereby he could get £1.25 in credit for every £1.17 he spent on bananas. The result was that he spent nearly £370 on 942lb of bananas and ended up in the papers. Or there’s Nige Billingham, a management consultant by day, who documents his holiday travel in detail on The Billingham Blog, including numerous “points runs” from Heathrow to Sofia, Bulgaria, and back, in some cases repeating the journey the following day, in order to maintain his BA Gold Guest List status.

Today there are whole sections of the internet showing ways to maximise your loyalty. Last year, husband-and-wife team Sam and Helena Eastwood started Points Well Made, which shares tips – through a website and social media accounts – for navigating this complicated world. They were inspired to do it by friends asking them how they had managed to pay for business-class return flights for a trip to LA.

“We’d say it was points, and people would look back at us with a sense of bafflement,” Sam says. “There was this knowledge gap. In the cost of living crisis, there are lots of people whose pound is not going as far. There are lots of ways you can subsidise your life for no extra charge, whether that be air miles or cashback or couponing.”

He says they have had good feedback from their followers. “Our audience isn’t 150,000-plus financiers in central London. We’re talking to families and everyday people. There is a stigma around asking about points. It’s oversaturated with loyalty schemes these days. Every shop does them. Half of them are a load of rubbish. Asda and Waitrose, you don’t get any proper rewards.” For most people starting out, he says, travel is the end goal, which is where the British Airways American Express card comes in. On the BA website, Avios fans boast of putting entire kitchen refurbs on their BA credit card to accumulate points. The trick is then finding the flights to the places you want at the times you need. One devotee stayed up until midnight (when the new flights drop every day), every night for two whole weeks in January to try to book flights to “anywhere hotter than here” for the following December. But the mission was simply impossible. The lesson being: points don’t always mean prizes.

data.title: German strikes hit Mercedes and BMW
data.description:
German carmakers are battling a wave of strikes as they clash with unions on pay.

Mercedes-Benz was braced for walkouts on Monday after disruption at BMW and Audi on Friday after IG Metall, Germany’s biggest union, called its first 24-hour strikes in eight years.

The union is seeking a new deal on pay as firms take action to rein in costs amid the onslaught from China.

Nearly 24,000 workers across northern Germany will down tools on Monday at plants owned by Mercedes and other industrial giants in a dispute about wages.

It comes after around 12,300 metal and electrical workers walked out on Friday in southern Germany.

The latest action threatens production of up to 10 Mercedes models in Bremen, including the best-selling C-Class saloon and GLC SUV, and the supply of parts from a plant in Hamburg.

Audi, whose owner Volkswagen is pressing for 120,000 job cuts, saw its main plant in Ingolstadt in Bavaria affected on Friday.

IG Metall has called the measures at Europe’s biggest carmaker, which suffered a €6bn (£5bn) loss in the third quarter, a “catalogue of horrors” and claimed that “management is stabbing its employees in the back”.

Three sites in Bavaria operated by BMW, which wants to eliminate 8,000 jobs, were also hit.

Mercedes is targeting €800m in savings as it pushes for longer working hours alongside reduced benefits and suspends future investments in Germany.

IG Metall is seeking a 5pc pay rise for 3.7 million workers, including those in the automotive sector, but says employers have offered only a €700 one-off payment plus a 1.3pc increase delayed until 2028 and amounting to a reduction in real wages.

Christiane Benner, the union’s president, said the 24-hour walkouts, which came after shorter stoppages earlier this month, amounted to “warning strikes” that could be followed by more disruption.

She said: “The employees’ frustration and concerns are so great that we are now stepping up our efforts. Workers are angry about the below-par offer and the lack of commitment to jobs and facilities.”

Friday’s walkouts extended beyond carmakers to 151,000 workers at more than 100 companies, including car-parts suppliers Robert Bosch and ZF Group, as well as manufacturers in the aerospace, rail, electrical goods and household appliances sectors.

The strikes on Monday will also hit Siemens Gamesa, which makes wind turbines, and the shipbuilder Meyer Werft, which makes some of the world’s largest cruise vessels.

The German Association of the Automotive Industry warned in July of collapsing employment unless workers accepted “bold decisions” to address competition from China.

Chinese brands captured 12pc of the European car market in the three months to June, double the previous year’s share.

data.title: Taxman loses out as TalkTalk collapse leaves £2bn trail of debt
data.description:
The taxman is among dozens of creditors facing significant losses after TalkTalk collapsed under £2bn worth of debts, new documents show.

The stricken broadband provider owed around £41m in VAT when it fell into administration last month, according to Alvarez & Marsal.

The insolvency firm said HMRC may recoup some of the money, but warned the exact amount was yet to be determined.

TalkTalk was scooped out of administration by BT in a takeover in October that saved 900 jobs.

The deal was valued at £400m although filings show that the company’s assets were only worth £3m. The rest of the purchase price involvement repayment of TalkTalk’s debts, meeting staff costs and absorbing future losses.

BT acquired TalkTalk following intervention by ministers who were concerned that the company’s collapse could leave tens of thousands of vulnerable customers in limbo.

The broadband provider, which served 2.5 million customers, had been racing to find a buyer as it struggled under a ballooning debt pile.

As well as money owed to the taxman, new filings show the scale of the money owed to investors in the City, as well as industry rivals and other suppliers.

TalkTalk’s largest industry creditor was BT, to which it owed around £125m, largely related to the cost of using the former monopoly’s Openreach network.

It also owes £80m to CityFibre, which operates a rival network, while Microsoft and mobile network Three are among other companies left millions of pounds out of pocket.

Overall, TalkTalk owes more than £300m to unsecured creditors, all of which is expected to be wiped out.

The majority of TalkTalk’s debt – around £1.5bn – is owed to banks, bondholders and other City investors that backed the company.

Ares, the private credit giant that was TalkTalk’s biggest lender and a major shareholder, is understood to have received around £100m as part of the transaction.

However, it is not expected to recoup hundreds of millions more it invested in the business. Private equity firm KKR was repaid the £62.5m it was owed in full.

The administrator’s latest filings underscore how financial troubles at TalkTalk, which was founded by entrepreneur Sir Charles Dunstone, stretch back years.

TalkTalk and Ares first appointed Alvarez & Marsal in November 2023 amid concerns about its liquidity. The following year, Sir Charles and Ares were forced to pump £235m into the company to stave off a looming debt default.

A&M continued to work with the ailing broadband provider, however, with their responsibilities extended to contingency planning this summer as the prospect of a sale became “increasingly more challenging”.

The filings show that TalkTalk received more than a dozen takeover bids after putting its consumer business and wholesale division, Platform X, up for sale. These included one offer that valued the entire company at £565m.

But by September these bids had dwindled, with one from private equity firm Epiris contingent on Openreach writing off around £100m in debt.

On Oct 2, Openreach refused to write off the debt and its parent company BT submitted a rival bid the same day.

In their report, the administrators said: “Following careful assessment, we concluded that this offer was the only option capable of being implemented in the timeframe available, and therefore the only realistic alternative to an insolvent liquidation of the group and the value-destructive consequences.”

BT’s swoop on TalkTalk proved controversial after Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, reserved the right to waive competition concerns using pandemic-era laws designed to maintain public health.

The move triggered complaints from rivals including Virgin Media O2, which branded the deal a “stitch-up”.

The competition regulator has presented a report on the deal to Ms Nandy, who is expected to issue a final decision shortly on whether BT’s acquisition is rubber-stamped.

Alvarez & Marsal and HMRC declined to comment.

data.title: Fans feel ‘played’ if films split books in two, says Hunger Games producer
data.description:
Cinema-goers “feel played” when books are split into two films, a producer for the Hunger Games has admitted.

Nina Jacobson said she regretted the trilogy’s two-part grand finale, adding that audiences felt “cynical” over the decision.

Mockingjay, the final book in Suzanne Collins’s extended trilogy, was released as two films in 2014 and 2015.

Ms Jacobson told Empire: “Mockingjay was such a big book, and it takes you to so many different places.

“But in the end, I think that Francis and I both felt that splitting them up… even if it did come from an inside-out place of really feeling like we needed two films to tell the story, I think audiences find it cynical. Even if its intentions are earnest, which they were.

“They feel like it’s a play to make them see two films instead of one.”

She added: “Even though I love the Mockingjay films, if I had it to do over again, I think both Francis [Lawrence, director] and I might try to do it all in one.”

The Hunger Games was not the first series to get the two-part treatment for its finale. Harry Potter and The Deathly Hallows, the last book of JK Rowling’s series, was split into two films in 2010 and 2011.

The finale of Stephenie Meyer’s Twilight series, Breaking Dawn, was also divided into two in 2011 and 2012.

Sunrise on the Reaping, the second prequel to The Hunger Games, hit screens last week.

The film generated $15m (£11.4m) at the box office during the five-day Thanksgiving holiday in the US, according to Variety.

Ms Jacobson said producers increasingly tried not to take advantage of the audience’s “patience”.

She said: “We really put the burden on ourselves [now], even when it’s a big book, to transform it into a theatrical experience, to not take advantage of your audience’s patience, to make it as tight as we can.”

Movies are changing for young people

Hollywood stars have complained that young people cannot watch films properly because of their waning attention spans.

Matt Damon complained that his own children played with their phones instead of watching the screen during his film Stillwater in 2021.

“Movies as we know them aren’t going to be a thing in our kids’ lives. And that makes me sad,” he said at the time.

Almost half of the time (44 per cent) UK adults spend watching, reading or listening to commercial media is now spent alone, according to figures from advertising trade body the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising earlier this year.

That figure is 10 percentage points higher than in 2015. It means adults now spend just over two-and-a-half hours consuming media on their own each day.

data.title: Hundreds of pharmacies face closure from Labour tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of pharmacies are facing closure because of soaring business rates, with owners warning that high taxes are forcing them to cut services for vulnerable patients.

Almost half of the 420 pharmacy owners surveyed by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said they were considering shutting down their practices because of higher business rates bills.

The trade body warned that pharmacies, many of which are family-run businesses, are unable to offset the higher tax burden by raising prices, which are fixed by the NHS.

The NPA found 55pc of pharmacy operators were considering moving to cheaper premises, raising fears that some rural and coastal communities could be left without a local branch.

Andy Burnham has made lowering business rates for high-street businesses a key pillar of his summer policy blitz, announcing a 20pc reduction for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, pharmacies have been excluded from the relief.

The tax squeeze has intensified since business rates were increased for many properties after Rachel Reeves’s second Budget. Bills have also been affected by the latest revaluation of commercial property.

GPs and NHS dentists, meanwhile, have their business rates reimbursed.

Pharmacies are particularly exposed because most of their income comes from the NHS, meaning they cannot simply raise prices to cover higher costs. Roughly 90pc of pharmacies’ income comes from the health service, the NPA said.

Onkar Singh, who runs 20 pharmacies across the Black Country, Staffordshire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, has seen his business rates bill rise by roughly 20pc to 30pc in the past year. His total bill is now about £250,000.

He has closed two of his pharmacies in the past two years and reduced opening hours across virtually his entire estate. He has also been forced to cut back services, such as offering free medicine deliveries to elderly patients.

Mr Singh said: “The last three years have been the worst period in my 30 years of pharmacy.

“People are having to close a lifetime’s worth of work and effort, and having to close or reduce hours or dip into their pension pot just to keep going for their communities.”

The NPA survey found that 92pc of pharmacies said their rates bill was preventing them from investing in their workforce or renovations. Some pharmacists have warned that their bills have tripled.

Mr Singh said the impact was particularly painful because pharmacies were often being asked to fill gaps elsewhere in the NHS.

He said: “It is frustrating that pubs and restaurants get the headlines, but pharmacies are actually delivering care.

“The NHS accepted that pharmacy did an exceptional job, but in terms of funding and support with business rates we seem to be forgotten.”

The NPA said 44 pharmacies had already closed this year, leaving the national network at its smallest since 2006.

Nine in 10 council areas have lost at least one pharmacy since 2022.

Olivier Picard, the chairman of the trade group, said pharmacies should receive the same rates treatment as GPs and dentists, arguing that they provide an essential health service.

A government spokesperson said: “Pharmacies already benefit from our wider business rates reforms, including permanently lower multipliers and our £4.3bn package to support ratepayers – and the government has increased funding for the sector by £340m this year as part of our shift to bring care closer to home.”

data.title: Grid operator handed £1bn Treasury loan to meet soaring wasted wind costs
data.description:
Britain’s grid operator has been forced to seek a £1bn loan from the Treasury to meet soaring wasted wind payments.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso), the body responsible for keeping the lights on, has been granted extra taxpayer support after the bill for so-called balancing costs hit £2bn this year.

That is up from £1.5bn in 2025. Neso has to commit ever-growing amounts to pay wind farms to switch off when the grid cannot cope with their output.

This is alongside payments to gas-fired power stations to replace lost power.

Neso confirmed its request for extra cash on Thursday, saying it had struck a “time-limited extension of a working capital facility from £700m to £1.7bn”.

It comes after the windy autumn weather pushed up balancing costs to £740m in October alone.

Typically, Neso recoups this money from energy bills. But balancing costs are now rising more quickly than the grid operator can recover the cash.

Wind farms are typically shut off because of transmission bottlenecks on the wires connecting Scottish turbines with households south of the border.

The low capacity of those transmission lines means excessive power can cause overheating, forcing turbines to be deactivated to avoid damage when it is too windy. Wind farm operators are then compensated as a result.

However, the main costs are incurred in paying gas-fired stations in southern England to fire up to compensate for the missing wind power.

This is always expensive but is currently made worse by the surge in gas prices caused by the Iran war.

The normal wholesale price of power is around £170 per megawatt hour, but Neso has been forced to pay significantly more over the past three months.

The Telegraph revealed earlier this month that Neso was paying around £1,500 per megawatt hour to at least three power stations.

‘Labour’s obsession with net zero’

Kathryn Porter, an analyst, said the costs had also been amplified by Neso’s failures to forecast supply and demand accurately.

She said: “The scale of the forecasting failure is extraordinary. Neso knows about transmission constraints and has forecasts of wind output and demand well before delivery.

“Where substantial wind curtailment is inevitable, arranging it in advance would allow wholesale prices to reflect the electricity that can actually be delivered.”

Balancing costs are common, but they have spiralled in the UK because so many wind farms were built in rural areas where there is not enough grid capacity to carry their output.

Greg Jackson, the chief executive of Octopus Energy, said: “This is yet another symptom of the failure to reform the electricity market, and it all falls on energy users at a time we’re already paying eye-watering prices.”

Richard Tice, Reform UK’s energy spokesman, said Labour’s focus on renewables such as wind power was exposing households and businesses to ever-greater costs.

He said: “Grid operator Neso has to borrow £1bn more from Treasury to keep the lights on by paying double: compensating wind farms not to turn off and begging gas generators to turn on.

“This is entirely due to Labour’s obsession with net zero that is making everyone poorer and killing jobs.”

Neso said the Treasury loan did not reflect the organisation’s underlying financial position.

A spokesman said: “We have agreed an extension to our working capital arrangements, allowing current balancing tariffs to remain unchanged and providing predictability for suppliers and their customers for the remainder of the charging year.”

John Constable, of the Renewable Energy Foundation, said: “Neso is having to borrow to pay a constraint bill that has spiralled because successive governments connected wind farms far faster than the grid needed to carry their output.

“The only lasting reform is to stop compensating wind generators for constraints they could have foreseen, so that the cost falls on developers rather than on bill payers and now taxpayers.”

data.title: Jim Ratcliffe to sell Ineos car factory to China’s BYD
data.description:
Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s car company is poised to sell its European factory to Chinese giant BYD before a major relocation to the US.

Ineos Automotive said on Tuesday that it had entered exclusive talks to sell the site in Hambach, north-eastern France, which it expected to offload early next year.

At the same time, the company revealed it was close to securing a manufacturing site in the US and aimed to begin production there from 2028.

The shake-up would mean Ineos Automotive’s Grenadier and Quartermaster four-by-fours were no longer hit by Donald Trump’s 15pc import tariffs in the US – the carmaker’s biggest market.

Producing in the US would result in “significant efficiencies, improve the company’s commercial performance and accelerate its growth worldwide”, Ineos said in a statement.

Meanwhile, BYD’s decision to acquire factory space in France is a fresh sign of the manufacturer’s ambition on the Continent and comes as the EU imposes import restrictions on Chinese hybrid cars.

If a sale went through, Ineos said it would continue to produce cars in Hambach “in the medium term” until its US facility was up and running.

Lynn Calder, the chief executive of Ineos Automotive, said: “This is arguably the biggest moment in the history of Ineos Automotive.

“Americans have already taken the Grenadier to their hearts and US policies have created an incredibly attractive, pro-growth business environment.

“Setting up production there makes so much sense. It will empower us to invest, expand and reach even more customers around the world.”

Inspired by the Land Rover Defender, Ineos launched the Grenadier four years ago and currently makes the station wagon – along with the Quartermaster pick-up variant – in France.

Since the Trump administration’s imposition of tariffs on European cars, the company has been scrambling to relocate production to the US.

It warned that the duties had an “adverse impact” on sales in 2025, which fell 15pc. The company’s losses also ballooned from €290m to €701m.

The Grenadier starts at $71,750 (£54,700) and has become popular in the US, where the rugged, boxy SUV competes with models such as the Toyota Land Cruiser, Mercedes-Benz G-Class and the Defender.

By comparison, Chinese carmakers are effectively excluded from the US market by swingeing tariffs and strict controls on “connected car” components that are made in China.

But they are proving highly competitive in Europe, where brands such as BYD are undercutting traditional carmakers with lower prices and comfortable, gadget-packed vehicles.

From January to October this year, BYD sold 237,137 cars across Europe – up from 94,557 during the same period last year – according to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association.

The EU has sought to clamp down on the flood of cheap Chinese cars, which it argues has been unfairly subsidised by Beijing, with tariffs on electric models and a new import quota for hybrids.

Major manufacturers such as Volkswagen and Stellantis have also announced factory closures and workforce cuts in an effort to slash costs and become more competitive.

However, analysts have warned that the EU’s trade measures may not be enough to slow the Chinese onslaught, particularly as companies such as BYD and Chery seek to establish factories on the Continent to avoid restrictions.
