data.title: How to avoid buying a new-build nightmare
data.description:
Buying a brand-new home can avoid the many issues that can come with purchasing an older property – the draughts, irregularly shaped rooms and restrictions that come with being listed, to name just a few.

While they come at a premium, once you’re in, new-builds should be more energy-efficient and built for the modern world. But the reality isn’t always so straightforward.

Almost 94pc of new-build homeowners reported defects or snags to their developer after moving in, according to the Home Builders Federation. HomeSnag, a new-build inspection company, said the average new home has around 130 defects.

Tim Phillips, quantity surveyor expert for the Homebuilding & Renovating Show, said: “One of the biggest misconceptions with buying a new-build is that because everything is brand new, the standard of the construction and workmanship must automatically be high. Unfortunately, that isn’t always the case.”

So, what are the key things to look out for before signing on the dotted line? And if you’re buying off-plan, how can you make sure the housebuilder isn’t turning out shoddy homes? We’ve spoken to property experts to find out.

Pick your developer carefully

When it comes to new-builds, it’s not just the property you’ll need to scrutinise – you should look into the developer, too.

A builder’s “customer satisfaction rating” from the Home Builders Federation can be a useful starting point to look into the company’s track record. But don’t assume a good rating guarantees a trouble-free purchase.

Nick Mendes, of the mortgage broker John Charcol, said: “Even highly rated developers can hand over homes with problems. Be sure to read independent reviews and, if possible, visit a development the same builder completed a year or two ago.”

As part of your due diligence, it can also be useful to speak to the people already living on the development about their experiences.

Mr Mendes added: “Residents will tell you far more about how quickly problems are fixed than any sales brochure or star rating.”

Check for warranties and buyer protections

Defects and problems can happen – but if they do, you’ll want to make sure they’re covered in some way. As a starting point, make sure the property comes with a recognised 10-year new-build warranty, such as NHBC Buildmark, Premier Guarantee or LABC Warranty.

Mr Mendes said: “Most mortgage lenders will not lend on a new-build without an approved warranty in place.”

You should also check whether the developer is registered with the New Homes Quality Board (NHQB), an independent body set up in 2022, to improve protection for new-build buyers.

Registration is still voluntary, so not every housebuilder is signed up. However, those that are must follow the NHQB Code of Practice which sets standards for build quality, customer service and complaints handling.

Crucially, this also gives you access to the New Homes Ombudsman Service if you cannot resolve a complaint directly with your developer.

Daniel Clarke, founder of the buying agent Homebuyer.Agency, said: “When considering a new-build, be sure to check exactly what the new-home warranty covers, who is responsible for resolving defects – and whether the developer falls under the New Homes Ombudsman scheme.”

Look beyond the show-home finish

If you’re viewing either the property you’re planning to buy or the developer’s show-home version, try not to get distracted by the “gloss”.

Mr Phillips said: “I would encourage buyers to look beyond the attractive kitchens, bathrooms and freshly decorated interiors, and consider the actual quality of the building itself.”

He explained that developers usually operate within carefully controlled construction budgets and programmes, often with pressure to manage costs and deliver properties on time.

Mr Phillips said: “While this is normal within the industry, problems can arise where cost savings or rushed workmanship compromise the finished product.”

He urged buyers to pay particular attention to the quality of the external brickwork, roof coverings, windows, doors, insulation, ventilation, drainage and the internal finishes.

Mr Phillips warned: “One of my biggest concerns with new-builds isn’t necessarily the defects you can see, but those you can’t. Poorly installed insulation, inadequate waterproofing, defective construction detailing and poorly executed drainage – can remain hidden for months, or even years.”

By the time these defects become apparent, the cost of putting them right can be substantial.

“It’s also important to understand that building control approval does not necessarily mean every aspect of the construction has been inspected or that the quality of workmanship is satisfactory,” he added. “My advice would be to treat a new-build with the same level of scrutiny as an older home.”

Check the small print before buying off-plan

If you’re making a purchase before a property has been built, you’ll be relying on the contract, rather than what you can see before you.

Mr Phillips said: “Buying off-plan introduces another layer of risk because you are committing substantial sums of money to a home before you’ve had the opportunity to inspect the finished building.”

The most important thing is establishing precisely what you’re paying for.

“I would strongly recommend obtaining a detailed written specification covering the proposed construction materials, insulation, heating system, windows, doors, kitchens, bathrooms, flooring, fixtures and external finishes,” he added.

Remember, a beautifully presented show home is effectively a marketing tool, not necessarily an accurate representation of what you will receive.

Before exchanging contracts, ask your solicitor to establish what changes the developer is entitled to make during construction – and what rights you have if substantial changes are proposed.

Make sure the plans and specification you have been shown are properly reflected in the contract, and that any promises made by the sales team are recorded in writing.

Another term to watch out for is a “reservation fee”. This can be several hundred pounds or more to secure a new-build property and can apply whether you’re buying off-plan, or one that’s already completed.

The terms – including whether the fee is refundable if you pull out, or if your mortgage falls through – can vary between developers. Be sure to go through this with a fine-tooth comb before parting with any cash.

Note that where the NHQB Code of Practice applies, buyers must be given a 14-day cooling-off period, during which they can cancel and receive a full refund of the reservation fee.

Don’t let building delays catch you out

Another important consideration when purchasing off-plan is the construction timetable and whether the developer is allowing enough time to complete the work properly.

Mr Phillips said: “Housebuilders often work to demanding completion targets, and problems can arise when subcontractors are rushed, work is poorly coordinated, or insufficient time is allocated for inspections and quality control.”

Be sure to ask about the anticipated completion date, how progress will be communicated, and whether there will be opportunities to view the property during construction.

Mr Phillips added: “Where possible, taking ‘progress photos’ of important stages can be useful, particularly before insulation, pipework and other concealed elements are covered up.”

You should also ask your conveyancer to check the “long-stop date”. This provision sets out how long the developer has to finish the home before you can potentially walk away.

Scrutinise incentives

Compared with similar existing homes nearby, new-builds often come with incentives such as paid legal fees or a contribution towards the deposit.

While on the surface, these can make a property appear more affordable, they can backfire. That’s because your mortgage lender will want to know about any incentives you’ve received.

Mr Mendes added: “If the lender’s valuation comes in below the price agreed with the developer, the buyer will need to make up the difference or renegotiate.”

Arrange an independent snagging inspection

If the developer allows it, get one of these set up before completion. Buyers should be offered the opportunity where the NHQB code applies. If this isn’t possible, book one as soon as you can afterwards.

A professional inspector can spot problems that you might miss as a buyer. Having these documented in writing at an early stage makes it much harder for the developer to delay putting them right.

Mr Clarke said: “An independent professional snagging inspection is one of the most valuable safeguards available.”

It’s also important to understand how your new-build warranty works, as while most last for 10 years, the level of protection offered typically changes over this period.

Mr Mendes said: “Most warranties cover defects and ‘snags’ reported to the developer within the first two years, so keeping a clear record of every issue and response from day one, is essential.”

Note that for the remaining eight years, the builder is no longer responsible for any issues, though homeowners can appeal to warranty providers who serve as a form of insurance.

Be under no illusion, though: warranties are not comprehensive guarantees against every defect.

Mr Clarke warned: “A 10-year warranty doesn’t mean every problem is covered for 10 years, and buyers shouldn’t assume that every issue will automatically be put right.”

Equally, should a dispute arise, independent advice and a clear written record of any problems can make a big difference to the outcome.

data.title: Poundstretcher’s US owner plots sale in new threat for high street
data.description:
The high street discount retailer Poundstretcher is being lined up for a sale by its US owners just a day after its larger rival Poundland collapsed into administration.

New York-based Fortress Investment Group, which also owns the Punch Pubs chain, is expected to start seeking a buyer for all or part of Poundstretcher as soon as Monday.

It comes just a day after Poundland declared itself insolvent. Its US owner Gordon Brothers failed to find a buyer for the business.

Poundstretcher, which has around 300 stores employing 3,000 people, has run into tough trading in recent years. The last set of published accounts showed it posted a £43.8m loss in the year to June 2025.

Fortress has provided tens of millions of pounds of funding to the retailer and has indicated it would be prepared to write off the debt to make a deal more likely, according to Bloomberg.

The uncertainty about the future of the chain brings yet more volatility to Britain’s struggling high streets despite Andy Burnham’s pledge to make reviving town centres one of his top priorities. The Prime Minister has previously said town centres have been “hollowed out” by decades of decline and become “unrecognisable”.

Discount chains such as Poundstretcher and Poundland operate on wafer-thin margins highly exposed to rising costs such as above-inflation increases in the minimum wage.

Poundland’s struggles have made life even harder for Poundstretcher as suppliers demand faster or immediate payment. A large-scale liquidation of Poundland’s stock would put further pressure on the Fortress-owned firm, according to sources cited by Bloomberg.

Fortress bought Poundstretcher in 2024 and backed a major restructuring this year. The investment firm has committed significant funding to trying to turn Poundstretcher around since acquiring the business.

Under the plan approved by the High Court in June, landlords faced steep rent cuts, while about £8.9m of inter-company debt was written off.

Fortress had provided about £20.4m of funding to the business and made available a loan facility of as much as £30m, according to the court judgment. As well as Poundland and Poundstretcher, WH Smith’s former high street business TG Jones is also being prepared for a sale process starting early next year.

Fortress and Poundstretcher declined to comment.

data.title: Falklands oil contractors down tools after threats from Argentina
data.description:
Contractors working for a British oil driller in the Falklands have downed tools following threats from Argentina.

Rockhopper, the UK-listed oil and gas company, said on Friday that two suppliers had quit in the wake of Javier Milei’s threats to sanction companies drilling off the Falkland Islands.

The contractors had been working on the Sea Lion oilfield, which is a joint venture between Rockhopper and Israel’s Navitas.

A Navitas spokesman confirmed that “they would not perform work on the project in light of Argentina’s activity to impose sanctions, among others, against contractors involved”.

It highlighted a “significant escalation” in aggression by the Argentine government in recent months, specifically against the Sea Lion project.

It comes after Mr Milei threatened in September to sue the British government if the project wasn’t scrapped within a two-week timeframe.

At the time, Navitas and Rockhopper called on Ed Miliband, the Foreign Secretary, to step up support for the project.

Mr Milei, who is a close ally of Donald Trump, claims that Argentina has sovereignty over the Falkland Islands and has declared that the Sea Lion project is “the illegal plundering of our resources”.

His position has been rejected by both the UK and Falkland Islands governments.

Mr Miliband has declared that “the islands are British” and that the UK’s position is “unwavering”.

But the issue has become a diplomatic flashpoint after Mr Trump said he was reviewing America’s position over British sovereignty of the Falklands.

The Sea Lion oilfield, which holds up to 1.7 billion barrels of oil, was discovered by Rockhopper in 2010.

It has since partnered with Navitas to secure more funding for the project.

Navitas said the partnership was in “advanced processes” to replace the two contractors and that “no material adverse effect is expected on the project and its schedules”. Production is expected to start in the first half of 2028.

Navitas and Rockhopper are operating under licenses granted by the Falkland Islands government with the support of the UK Government.

Although the Argentine government has said it has filed criminal complaints against the joint venture and its subsidiaries, Navitas said it is not aware of any formal indictments that have been filed against them.

The Argentine government has also announced the expansion of administrative sanctions against the joint venture and its suppliers.

However, a Navitas spokesman said: “As of the date of approval of the report, no official notice regarding the opening of these proceedings against it has been served to the partnership.”

“The partnership, with the assistance of its legal advisors, is monitoring developments and will act, as required, as it sees fit.”

data.title: Chairman of major housebuilder quits as crunch talks with lenders loom
data.description:
The chairman of one of Britain’s best-known housebuilders is to quit as fears grow over a debt crunch at the group.

Crest Nicholson, the FTSE 250 developer, said on Thursday that Iain Ferguson would stand down as chairman at its annual meeting in March.

The move comes as the company enters urgent talks with lenders to shore up its troubled balance sheet after a downturn in trading.

Shares in the group fell to a record low this week after it warned investors to brace for a loss of between £30m and £40m this year, higher than the £10m loss that was previously expected.

The exit of Mr Ferguson, the former boss of Tate & Lyle, threatens to worsen the turmoil at the developer as it works through negotiations with lenders before a refinancing deadline next week.

Crest Nicholson has issued a string of profit warnings over the past year because of a slowdown in the UK’s property market, which has heavily affected UK developers.

Higher mortgage rates have hit demand for new homes at a time when rising costs and regulatory burdens have made housebuilding more difficult.

New figures released on Thursday showed housebuilding has fallen to its lowest level in a decade, with just 203,690 new builds last year.

Crest Nicholson’s main competitors – including Taylor Wimpey, Bellway and Barratt Redrow – have also bemoaned the slow pace of housebuilding and cut their construction targets.

Crest Nicholson’s shares are down by more than two thirds over the past year.

The housebuilder had roughly £64m worth of debt at the end of October, a sum lower than the £70m to £90m in debts that it had previously anticipated.

Defects in some of Crest Nicholson’s buildings have also left the construction company facing millions of pounds’ worth of repair bills, which have added to its woes.

The housebuilder has faced further costs related to fixing cladding in the wake of the Grenfell Tower fire. It agreed to replace cladding on a number of buildings under a deal with the former Conservative government in 2022.

The problems have seen Crest Nicholson become a target of short-sellers who have bet heavily against its shares, making it one of the UK’s most shorted companies.

Started in 1963, Crest Nicholson is one of Britain’s biggest housebuilders, with major developments across the South of England, the Midlands and Yorkshire.

The company completed 1,691 new homes in the 2025 financial year and a further 584 new houses in the first half of 2026.

Crest Nicholson’s main competitors – including Taylor Wimpey, Bellway and Barratt Redrow – have also bemoaned the slow pace of housebuilding and cut their construction targets.

Crest Nicholson’s shares are down by more than two thirds over the past year.

The housebuilder had roughly £64m worth of debt at the end of October, a sum lower than the £70m to £90m in debts that it had previously anticipated.

Defects in some of Crest Nicholson’s buildings have also left the construction company facing millions of pounds’ worth of repair bills, which have added to its woes.

The housebuilder has faced further costs related to fixing cladding in the wake of the Grenfell Tower fire. It agreed to replace cladding on a number of buildings under a deal with the former Conservative government in 2022.

The problems have seen Crest Nicholson become a target of short-sellers who have bet heavily against its shares, making it one of the UK’s most shorted companies.

Started in 1963, Crest Nicholson is one of Britain’s biggest housebuilders, with major developments across the South of England, the Midlands and Yorkshire.

The company completed 1,691 new homes in the 2025 financial year and a further 584 new houses in the first half of 2026.

data.title: Volvo loses £1bn in value as it slashes 2,500 jobs
data.description:
Volvo has announced plans to slash 2,500 jobs after a sharp fall in sales triggered a share price slump that has wiped £1bn from its value.

Shares in the company, which is owned by Chinese group Geely, plunged as much as 31pc after it revealed revenues fell by 23pc in the third quarter.

Volvo announced a 5bn Swedish kronor (£376.4m) cost-cutting plan that will result in around 2,000 job cuts in Sweden and another 500 globally “through natural attrition and by targeted exit packages to employees”.

The car manufacturer warned it may have to take “additional actions” after revenues in China fell by almost 50pc and it was hit by the loss of electric car subsidies in the US.

Volvo issued a profit warning and pulled its annual guidance earlier this month as sales declined.

Hakan Samuelsson, Volvo’s chief executive, said on Friday: “We continue to operate in a very tough environment with strong external challenges: de-globalisation, hypercompetition and climate change.

“The third quarter of 2026 was very disappointing and reflects a year that has become far more challenging than originally anticipated. Our ongoing turnaround plan therefore needs ​a decisive reinforcement.”

Volvo is the latest European car manufacturer to announce sweeping job losses. In July, BMW revealed it would cut 8,000 jobs in an attempt to reduce costs. Earlier this year, Volkswagen said it would cut as many as 100,000 roles out of a total workforce of 650,000. The move is expected to result in the closure of four factories.

Jaguar Land Rover, Britain’s largest car manufacturer, said in September that it would cut 4,000 jobs over the next two years.

Volvo’s revenues in the three months to the end of September slumped to 66.9bn Swedish kronor (£5bn), a 23pc decline from the same period a year earlier.

The car manufacturer also fell to a net loss of 5.7bn kronor (£429.2m) in the third quarter, down from a net profit of 4.5bn kronor (£338.8m) a year earlier.

Volvo, which had bet heavily on electric vehicle sales, said the axing of customer incentives in the US under Donald Trump had dented its revenue.

In 2024, the carmaker scrapped a target of transitioning to selling only electric cars by the end of the decade.

Last month, Volvo said that Mr Samuelsson would leave as chief executive next year, with Klaus Zellmer, the boss of Skoda Auto, due to take up the Volvo chief executive of the Swedish car manufacturer “no later” than October next year.

data.title: Janet Street-Porter: ‘Flicking a Brussels sprout in a disabled woman’s face was my career low’
data.description:
Janet Street-Porter, 79, is a journalist, broadcaster, television personality and former media executive.

Best memory from your younger years?

Going to clubs and hearing live music when I was around 14. I would go to rhythm and blues and soul clubs. I saw bands like Manfred Mann and the Yardbirds. It was fantastic. I can’t describe how good it was. I was so lucky to have grown up then. Being able to go and hear all those bands live and also a lot of blues artists like Muddy Waters and Lonnie Johnson. I was a mod. Then I was an R&B and jazz fan. Those were the best times for me.

Best advice you’ve ever received?

The problem for anyone taking a big new job is that some of the staff will be deeply resentful about the departure of the previous incumbent. The advice I was given before I went to address the troops when I became editor of the Independent on Sunday was: “One third will hate you. You can’t do anything about that. They’re just going to loathe you. One third will give you the time of day. You could persuade them. And one third will like you. You’ve got to focus on the third that you can win over, and then you’ll have a working majority.”

Best celebrity encounter?

David Bowie was very charming. He insisted we did it before he went on stage. I had to sit with him in his dressing room. We both had the same colour hair, which was a source of great amusement. We talked about hair dye. Then I walked with him right to the point where he went on the stage. With John Lydon, I interviewed him in a flat on Denmark Street, which he was sharing with others. I became quite friendly with him. He came to my 50th birthday. People were queuing up to be insulted by him. Everybody from John Birt, who was head of the BBC at the time, right through to Ruby Wax and loads of comedians. John [Lydon] is just such a charismatic character. I’ve done a lot of interviews, but to be honest, they can feel so staged. I don’t do any interviews now. They’re all about PR. Back then, it was about having a conversation.

Best habit?

Every morning, when I wake up, I drink a big cup of hot water with a slice of lemon in it. It makes me feel like I’ve done something good to start the day and it washes out whatever I ate the night before. My other good habit is, before I go to sleep every night, I do two things: I read a book for about 20 minutes no matter how tired I am. I read fiction because I find that it stops me thinking about the news and work and everything else. The other thing I do is I write a very short list of things I have to do the next day. When I tell people to do it I say: “Don’t write more than four. You don’t want to fail.”

Best thing about England?

The food. Black pudding and beautiful eggs. I never forget spending 24 hours in Benidorm for a story. In the course of 24 hours, I got completely trashed and ended up in a gay club. But the next morning, I remember seeing a sign that said “real eggs” which was just what I needed. I love real eggs. I love black pudding. I love bacon. I know it’s been demonised, but dry-cured British free-range back bacon is incredible. I grow quite a lot of my vegetables. With a salad, nothing tastes better than your own lettuce.

Worst childhood memory?

When my dad told my sister and I that we were moving the next Tuesday from the terraced house that we rented in Fulham, west London, to suburbia. I was 14 years old, I had just returned from school, and my dad said to my sister and I: “Right, girls, pack your bags. We’re moving on Tuesday.” No consultation, nothing. It was really hard. My sister changed schools because she was 12, so she started at a new school. But we moved to a characterless suburban estate where they had bought a semi-detached house at the end of a road. I couldn’t blame them. I mean, now they had a garden. My dad turned the bomb or air raid shelter at the bottom of our garden into a kind of den.

Worst advice you’ve ever received?

Be nice. Nice never gets you anywhere. I have learnt as I’ve grown older to appear nicer. I can be nice in social situations but in a work situation, where there’s a lot to play for – and there has been in my career – I have had to balance what I need to achieve with how I might appear.

Worst moment of your career?

I’ve been made redundant quite a few times. I was made redundant early on in my career when the Daily Mail went from broadsheet to tabloid. I was thrilled about that because I’d already lined up a job in the Evening Standard. So I got a payoff and I had another job. When I’ve been let go, I’ve not been that beaten up about it because I’ve always thought a career move is a good thing. It doesn’t mean going down. You might go sideways. We all know in the media that whoever goes up will surely come down. I used to get upset. I accept that one day, whoever is paying you will look at you and go: “We’ve had enough of you. Let’s have someone else.”

Worst moment of being on Loose Women?

A low moment was when, around Christmas time, they did a bit on the correct way to cook Brussels sprouts. They gave me this plate of sprouts live on television. I tasted one and I found them so disgusting. I flicked them and a woman in a wheelchair in the front row got a face full of Brussels sprouts. I was mortified. Afterwards, she kept saying: “It’s fine, it’s fine.” But I felt terrible.

Worst thing about England?

The constant meddling with all our town centres. One-way systems. Traffic systems. This year I’m going on tour again in September and it’ll go right through to April. I’ll go to 32 places around England and Scotland and I will discover in quite a few of them that in the middle of the town, no matter how beautiful and how lovely that town is, it’ll be dug up and in the process of being reimagined by a traffic planner. I won’t be able to walk around that town without seeing cones and ugliness.

Absolute worst thing ever?

Always being late when I’m trying to be on time. I have this recurring nightmare where I’m staying at Elton John’s house. Him and David Furnish say: “Get ready. We’re leaving now.” And in the dream, I run down the stairs and they’re all gone. If I don’t have it with Elton, I’ll have it with Neil Tennant. I’ll have the same dream over and over again that I’m somewhere with everyone and then everybody’s gone because I’ve messed about. I’ve looked in the mirror. I’ve tried on a watch. I’ve faffed about.

Since 2011, Janet Street-Porter has been a regular panellist on the ITV daytime talk show Loose Women. She has also made frequent appearances on Question Time and Have I Got News for You, and been a contestant on I’m a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! and Celebrity MasterChef. After a career in print journalism she held senior leadership roles at the BBC and, in 1988, won a Bafta for creating and editing Channel 4’s youth television series Network 7. She was awarded the CBE in 2016. On January 31, 2026, Street-Porter married her fifth husband, Peter Spanton, in Great Yarmouth, Norfolk.

Janet Street-Porter’s one woman show Still Off The Leash at 80 started this September and continues to April 2027. Details here.

data.title: Jolyon Maugham concedes defeat in battle with gender-critical barrister
data.description:
Jolyon Maugham KC has dropped a legal battle with a gender-critical barrister after admitting he would be unlikely to win in court.

The Good Law Project (GLP), which was founded by the prominent anti-Brexit campaigner, has ended its fight to have Sarah Phillimore, a family barrister, punished by the professional watchdog over a series of posts on social media.

The legal campaign group had planned to launch a judicial review against the Bar Standards Board (BSB), which regulates the barristers’ profession, after it refused to sanction Ms Phillimore for allegedly harassing a trans person online.

Mr Maugham’s group had complained to the BSB that Ms Phillimore had engaged in “harassment, bullying and/or discrimination”, including by allegedly “misgendering” a trans person in a series of posts on X.

However, the barristers’ watchdog rejected the Good Law Project’s complaint, saying Ms Phillimore had “the right to express her gender-critical beliefs” and that no further action would be taken.

The GLP said it had now decided to abandon its challenge against the regulator after being told by expert lawyers that a judicial review would be “unlikely to succeed”.

Ms Phillimore told The Telegraph: “The GLP campaign from the outset has been an unprincipled attack on my integrity and an attempt to punish me for daring to express ‘wrong think’ around the issues of sex and gender identity.”

The GLP was founded by Mr Maugham in 2017 to bring legal challenges against Brexit. However, it has since expanded its scope to campaign on trans issues.

Mr Maugham subsequently came to prominence for killing a fox with a baseball bat on Boxing Day in 2019 while wearing his wife’s kimono.

Earlier this year, the Good Law Project relocated its legal structure to Jersey in a move that handed ownership to a “purpose trust” registered under the offshore jurisdiction’s law.

The campaign group is funded through donations and generated more than £6m in income in 2026, according to its most recent annual report.

Ms Phillimore added: “The GLP have raised money from their donations to fund two attempts now to get the BSB to punish me. They need to be transparent in how much this has cost them. They have instructed leading counsel.”

Ms Phillimore has separately filed a £50,000 libel claim against Mr Maugham after he claimed she had “led a campaign of harassment of a trans woman so wicked that she sought to take her own life” in relation to the same case.

Mr Maugham is continuing to defend himself against Ms Phillimore’s defamation lawsuit, which was filed in the High Court earlier this year.

data.title: British baked beans ‘under threat from Burnham tariffs’
data.description:
British baked beans are under threat from Andy Burnham’s decision to cut tariffs on imported food, manufacturers have warned.

On Tuesday, the Government announced the suspension of tariffs on more than 100 food products, including cutting the 16 per cent levy on tinned beans.

The move was part of a package of measures the Chancellor announced in his Budget to give families “breathing space” amid the cost of living crisis.

However, British food bosses have warned that cheap exports from the US and China could undermine the country’s major bean processing industry.

The Heinz baked bean plant in Wigan, Greater Manchester, employs up to 850 people and produces 1.5 million tins a day. The Princes Group, which makes Branston baked beans, is owned by Italian food conglomerate Newlat and is one of Britain’s biggest food manufacturers with around 2,000 UK staff.

Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said Mr Healey’s Budget had done “nothing to ease the pressures food and drink manufacturers are under”.

“One of the Chancellor’s flagship announcements, removing tariffs from some food and drink products, will have no meaningful impact on consumer prices,” she said.

“But it will undermine British factories and their workers, grappling with much higher costs, producing the same products.”

A spokesman for the Princes Group said: “Based on our understanding of the proposals so far, removing tariffs on imported finished baked beans is unlikely to have a meaningful impact on prices, particularly as there are currently no tariffs on the imported haricot beans used by UK manufacturers and no tariffs on EU imports.

“We believe measures that help address the higher costs of manufacturing food in the UK, particularly energy costs, would have a greater impact for both consumers and British businesses.”

The tariff announcement was made days after the Prime Minister said he would put the British family favourite in his emergency box in case of a national disaster. Asked what items he would stockpile, he picked baked beans, soup and Twiglets.

The FDF said it was also concerned about the lifting of tariffs on boiled sweets, toffees and caramels and pressed sweets like Love Hearts and Parma Violets, as well as chocolate.

Last year, the UK and US both applied a tariff of up to a 10 per cent on chocolate imports from the other country. Since then, the US has increased its tariff to 20 per cent and the UK has just removed it for most products.

In addition, the FDF said there were concerns around jams, marmalades and purees, tomato ketchup, tomato sauces, soups and broths.

“Food and drink manufacturing should be central to the Government’s growth and reindustrialisation agenda,” said Ms Betts. “But time and again, we are treated as an afterthought.

“The Treasury, in particular, has persistently failed to recognise the importance of food and drink manufacturing to jobs and prosperity across the length and breadth of the UK.”

The FDF said that particular companies that could be affected, including confectioners Nestle in York and Halifax, Haribo in Bradford, and Cadbury in Bourneville and Tiptree jam in Colchester.

The Government says the tariff suspensions, taken together with others announced earlier this year, will reduce consumer costs by up to £595m a year, saving households up to £21 on their annual food shop.

In its response to a consultation on the changes, the Government said it recognised there “may be some limited impacts on domestic producers of goods”, but said it “considers the benefits of this to consumers, through reduced costs, outweigh those risks”.

data.title: Workers fear losing jobs over train delays, warn MPs
data.description:
Workers fear losing their jobs because rail services are regularly late, MPs have warned.

A spate of line closures and cancellations during the summer heatwaves made it impossible for thousands of commuters to arrive at the office on time.

MPs at a Westminster Hall debate said workers were increasingly fearful of the lack of reliable train connections and urged the Government to spend more on rail infrastructure to improve punctuality.

Charlotte Cane, the Liberal Democrat MP for Ely and East Cambridgeshire, said: “One [constituent] in particular has written to say that because their train has been so unreliable for getting to their job in London that their employer is now putting them under pressure.

“They are becoming an unreliable member of staff and their employer doesn’t know when they are going to turn up to work.

“They are also having to make up the time at the end of the day, which means they are getting home very late. It makes it a complete nightmare for them.”

Desperate to protect their jobs, some workers were now considering moving house to be closer to stations with more reliable services, MPs said.

Others are considering giving up well-paid positions in London and other major cities for less lucrative roles closer to home.

Among the worst-hit lines this summer was the route between King’s Cross and King’s Lynn via Cambridge and Ely, the later of which lies in Ms Cane’s constituency.

It suffered three months of disruption, including 900 cancellations after normally damp peat beneath the tracks dried out, leading the ground to become uneven.

James Wild, the Conservative MP for North West Norfolk, which includes King’s Lynn, said people from the town who worked in Cambridge and London had found the disruption intolerable.

He told The Telegraph: “I’ve had quite a number of constituents who have said they’re thinking of moving jobs. They’ve been in tears and incredibly stressed.

“One lady said her husband, who commutes and is self-employed, had been driven to depression and was having suicidal thoughts because he was worried that he wouldn’t be able to provide for his family. It’s pushing people to breaking point.”

Mr Wild said some commuters had opted to drive to Peterborough on the East Coast Main Line, or Norwich, which has trains to Liverpool Street – both an hour away by road – to be sure of getting to work.

He said there were concerns that with the line suffering heat-related disruption for the past two summers, people would stop viewing King’s Lynn as a viable commuter town, which could have a knock-on effect on house prices.

Mr Wild questioned Andy Burnham about the matter in September, when the Prime Minister said he would “convene a rail summit soon”.

Richard Foord, the Liberal Democrat MP for Honiton and Sidmouth, said commuters to cities beyond London had also been affected.

He said restrictions imposed between London Waterloo and the West Country had in one case led a dental hygienist to cancel her 9am appointments “indefinitely”.

Simon Lightwood, the minister for local transport, said he could not rule out further weather-related disruption.

He added that while speed restrictions and closures might be frustrating, the railway’s primary duty was to keep passengers safe.

data.title: Swiss face £9bn bill to keep trains running on time
data.description:
Switzerland’s trains are celebrated for their immaculate punctuality. But now the country is facing a £9bn bill to stop its rail services becoming like those in Germany, its erratic neighbour.

The country’s largest railway operator, state-owned SBB, has said its backlog of repairs to tracks and signal boxes rose 12pc last year to 9.5bn Swiss francs (£8.6bn).

If the repairs aren’t carried out, SBB has warned that Switzerland risks “a situation similar to that in other countries” – a reference to Germany, where the formerly clockwork-like train network has become notoriously unreliable.

So far, the Swiss trains are holding the line on their fabled punctuality. This year 94pc of its trains have arrived within three minutes of their scheduled time, about the same rate as the previous two years.

No other major European country gets above 90pc, and many have resorted to using a looser definition of punctuality.

Britain scored 84pc last year. Germany clocked 88pc, but that excludes cancelled trains and defines punctual as within six minutes. Even on that metric, just 60pc of Germany’s long-distance and high-speed trains run on time.

Germany’s decline arose from underinvestment in maintenance. As it tries to play catch-up, large sections of track often have to be closed for repairs, making punctuality even worse.

Switzerland will be keen to avoid that fate.

But SBB is at loggerheads with the Swiss government, which instead wants to spend 20bn Swiss francs (CHF).on expanding and embellishing the rail network.

This could include building a whole new station at Lucerne, at a potential cost of more than CHF 3bn, and a 17-mile tunnel with a potential budget of CHF 800m.

SBB, in a submission to a public consultation, urged the authorities to prioritise fixing the existing network over any major expansion.

Both sides agree, though, that the signalling system also needs a technological overhaul that will cost a further CHF 9bn.

This week SBB kicked off the first CHF 2bn tender for the IT revamp. The full digitalisation of signalling will cost another CHF 7bn by 2045, but so far the government has budgeted just CHF 1bn for this process.

Meanwhile, money is tight for the essential repairs to keep the trains running on time. SBB has said it needs to repair at least 143 miles of track a year, but last year only managed 116 miles.

Funding for its track and signalling work comes from a separate Rail Infrastructure Fund, which is bankrolled by annual contributions from the national and cantonal governments, alongside some hypothecated portions of VAT, income tax and the mineral oil tax. Some of this funding is due to expire in 2030.

data.title: The village shut down for 18 months by a forgotten mine
data.description:
Police banged on her front door at midnight and told Diana Nguyen that she, her husband and two children, 6 and 14, had to leave. There was no time to pack a bag. After a few fruitless hours spent trying full hotels, they found themselves huddled in their car, parked in a public car park, trying to sleep. It was February 2025, so they kept the engine running to keep warm. Nguyen struggled to comprehend the reality of where they found themselves, but particularly why.

A gaping sinkhole had started to collapse across the A-road just metres from their new-build home in the desirable Surrey village of Godstone. It would eventually spread to 20m. Nguyen, a nail technician, 44, says it felt as if she were living in a disaster movie, not the comfortable Home Counties.

“It was quite a small hole, then after around an hour it became bigger, and then after a couple of hours water was gushing (into it),” she recalls, describing the burst water pipe which emerged inside. “I couldn’t believe it was that massive; it felt like an avalanche. We just grabbed coats, passports, my daughter’s blanket. That’s all.”

She says they could not move back home for more than two months, only permitted to return briefly for belongings, and claims that around the first month they hopped between hotels and Airbnbs before Tandridge district council (TDC) provided a flat. “Often we didn’t have a place to cook. It was really stressful. My children were so stressed they couldn’t concentrate on their schoolwork,” she recalls.

A council spokesman says its “main responsibility involved providing emergency accommodation for the evacuated households that needed it, for as long as they needed it”. They say they found “accommodation where necessary”, and while some households returned home after four days, most were home by the end of March 2025, with the last returning in September 2025.

Godstone’s sinkhole made national headlines when it swallowed up an expanse of the village’s busy A25 high street late on Feb 17, 2025, reaching 20m by lunchtime the next day, before a smaller sinkhole collapsed across the road. Thirty properties were evacuated, with one homeowner escaping through a window.

When David White, infrastructure schemes team manager at Surrey county council (SCC), arrived on Feb 19, the “alarming” hole was “still growing in size as the unstable edges collapsed in”, he recalls. The second one went “without warning”, with both sinkholes displacing “several hundred tons of sand”. Godstone sits on sandstone – a point that was to become integral to investigations.

Godstone’s sinkholes effectively shut down the village for 18 months, cutting off businesses from passing trade and even villagers living on the other side of the holes. The road only reopened in July this year and two businesses remain shut.

Godstone’s sinkholes have now been featured in a BBC Two documentary, Why Sinkholes Collapse, sandwiched between global disasters including a 20m-deep, 30m-wide sinkhole which gaped across a busy highway in Bangkok, Thailand, in September 2025, taking power lines with it, and a 10m-deep sinkhole in Japan which swallowed a lorry and its driver.

Geologist Anthony Cooper explains these sinkholes were both man-made, whereas others can be naturally forming. In Bangkok and Japan, a malfunctioning subway tunnel and deteriorated sewer pipe respectively were below the sinkholes, while in the UK’s own “sinkhole capital”, Ripon, North Yorkshire, the area’s soluble gypsum rock means water dissolving it over many years causes it to organically form cavities. That is similar to limestone in an area such as the Pennines. In Surrey itself, White admits he is regularly called to natural sinkholes in chalky ground.

“You’ve got to have a cavity, whether it’s man-made or natural,” Cooper explains. “Adding water to that can help the material flow into those cavities, resulting in a sinkhole at the surface.” The world over we are seeing more sinkholes, he explains, due to extreme weather and human infrastructure, especially where it is ageing.

Godstone’s cavities were also man-made. Below the collapse was a labyrinth of long-forgotten sand mines, tunnelled in the 18th and 19th centuries, producing its famous silver sand valued for glassmaking and horticulture. The former industry here is well known, but White says these tunnels were unmapped, and he embarked on an eight-month investigation to discover where the sandy contents of the holes had gone.

A CCTV camera lowered down bore holes discovered the network, some 100m long, 8.5m below ground. Intricate imaging even revealed tool marks on the tunnel walls and soot where miners had hung their candles.

Loose sand was eventually found in a collapsed tunnel, thought to have been helped in its journey by escaping water from the burst pipe. Cooper explains water pipes and cavities usually play “chicken and egg”. “Geologists cannot differentiate between the ground collapsing and breaking the pipe and then causing a sinkhole with lots of water going in, or the pipe breaking and washing a lot of material in and causing a sinkhole,” he says, although he stresses he has not investigated Godstone.

No liability has been found for the sinkholes, meaning no compensation. SES Water says: “Investigations by independent experts confirmed the ground collapse in Godstone was caused by the failure of supporting pillars within historic mines due to erosion, resulting in a loss of ground support around our water main causing it to burst. While we are unable to comment on liability for the damage, we can confirm that the collapse was not caused by SES Water.”

White explains information was gathered “which we hope will help us to understand the cause”, but stresses “this investigation is still underway, and it would be inappropriate to speculate on the outcome, or whether any liability may be determined”.

Although he reiterates the precise location of mines on Godstone’s roads was not known, villagers express little surprise at their existence. Godstone sits on a maze of tunnels, they say. There is even a row of terraces called “Cave Cottages”. Stories abound of football being played in tunnels and brass bands practising there during the war. And in 1879, a horse and carriage fell into a sinkhole on the high street.

“There are some caves just two doors down which I used to play in when I was a child,” adds Bren Davis, 89. He and his wife refused to evacuate from their high-street home. His grandfather purposefully built the home on layers of bricks, he insists. “There are more bricks below the ground than above.”

Lesley Burnett, 86, who narrowly avoided evacuation this time, whispers conspiratorially: “This was not the first hole in the history of Godstone by any means.” She recalls one collapsing next to her allotment in the 1990s. “One Sunday morning there was suddenly a hole in our neighbour’s allotment. It was 20ft across and 12ft deep,” she says. “Her globe artichokes went on growing across the bottom, and in due course her husband helped her down on a rope and she harvested them.”

Certainly the village was not braced for the enormity of this one. Sami Bristow, 33, who owns Blossoms Brunch & Coffee, saw her year’s revenue fall 8 per cent. She was forced to close on Tuesdays as well as her usual Mondays, and remains so. Dipping into VAT funds to pay rent and wages, she missed the deadline and was fined. “It felt like there was a possibility we weren’t actually going to be able to get through this,” she says.

TDC offered a 100 per cent business rate discount to affected businesses, but Bristow claims she did not initially qualify as she wasn’t immediately next to the hole and only later received it. She says she would have welcomed more “apologies for the delays and how much it had affected us”. A TDC spokesman reiterated it “has given 100 per cent relief to all businesses directly affected on the high street” until March 31, 2027. SCC adds that once they led communications, “residents and businesses were updated on our highways works every month via letter door drops” and via drop-in sessions, social media platforms, its website and newsletter.

Shane Fry, 36, who owns the garage DD Services Ltd, fought to remain open. “I was having to collect [customers’] cars from the village and then drive them back down when they were finished,” he says. “We were only turning over about a quarter of what we should have been for about five months. I lost between £60-80,000.” Mark Cullinan, the landlord at The Hare and Hounds, adds: “The impact was ridiculous. We were down about 40 per cent for about 12 months. I reckon we’re still down at least 10-15 per cent.”

Homeowners fear financial impact, too. One resident confides she has had her new-build valued at a £40,000 loss.

An incredible 190 bore holes were drilled across the sinkhole area, the full network of tunnels beneath the road mapped, and 1,100 tons of grout injected into the tunnels. The engineering project cost £3.6m. Today, there appears no sign of these monumental efforts above ground, yet there is anxiety about a sinkhole opening again.

White insists “there are no longer any voids beneath the road in that location, so the risk of further collapse has been eliminated”, adding “overall, I think we did a phenomenal job to reopen the road as quickly as we did”.

However, he admits: “We could not survey the entirety of Godstone for potential voids at the same time”, adding that the process was “hugely invasive and time-consuming”. He reassures residents: “We know the vast majority of the historic mines are located away from the roads in the village, and many of them have been removed by open cast quarrying which superseded the old tunnelling techniques.”

Burnett has adopted the only attitude she believes she can. “I try not to think about it,” she says.

Why Sinkholes Collapse is available on iPlayer now

data.title: Perfume bosses ran cartel at ‘beer and curry’ meetings
data.description:
The bosses of some of the world’s biggest perfume makers colluded to fix prices during “beer and curry” meetings in London, the UK’s competition watchdog has said.

DSM-Firmenich, Givaudan and International Flavors & Fragrances (IFF), three of the world’s largest fragrance manufacturers, have been fined £85m by the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) for taking part in a years-long price-fixing cartel.

Executives at the Swiss and American firms shared sensitive information about their day-to-day dealings with Unilever, the British consumer goods company that owns brands including Domestos, Dove and Cif.

This was then used by the three companies to resist Unilever’s calls to lower prices for the chemical fragrances used in everything from shampoos to cleaning products to colognes, the CMA said.

The scheme saw senior staff swap information about their pricing strategies and negotiation tactics in exchanges on WhatsApp, phone calls and “beer and curry” meetings in London, the watchdog said.

The three conglomerates also agreed an embargo on poaching staff who were working on their respective Unilever accounts, to limit disruption to their teams and ensure their price-fixing schemes remained in place.

Staff at Givaudan and IFF are accused of going further by coordinating pricing more widely across their broader fragrance businesses, including by sharing information on internal targets for price increases.

‘Knock-on effects’

Juliette Enser, the CMA’s executive director of competition enforcement, said: “Suppliers must set their prices and commercial strategies independently of each other.

“Exchanging sensitive information with competitors can weaken competition and leave business customers facing costs. This may also have knock-on effects for consumers buying the final product, including the price they pay.”

The perfume giants were fined a further €471.9m (£400m) by the European Commission for their participation in the “international fragrance cartel” which operated for four years between 2019 and 2023.

The cartel was discovered and stopped in March 2023 when European Commission authorities carried out surprise office inspections, having previously launched an investigation on its own initiative.

The European Commission’s investigation was carried out in close co-operation with the Swiss Competition Commission and the US Department of Justice and the UK’s CMA.

All three firms were given discounts on their fines by both the CMA and the European Commission for co-operating with the investigations and settling with authorities.

Ms Enser added: “These were major international suppliers discussing information that should have remained confidential. Today’s fines should be a clear warning for all businesses: competitors must compete, not coordinate behind closed doors.”

DSM-Firmenich said it had “cooperated fully” with investigators and said the settlement represented “the company’s commitment to maintaining the highest standards of compliance and business conduct”. It said the settlement was not an admission of liability.

An IFF spokesman said that the company “has accepted responsibility for improper conduct involving certain individuals, none of whom remain with the company”.

Christian Stammkoetter, chief executive of Givaudan, said the behaviour identified by the regulators was “unacceptable”.

data.title: Kew Gardens to cut up to 90 jobs
data.description:
Kew Gardens is poised to cut up to 90 jobs after a rapid expansion left it vulnerable to a heatwave-induced downturn in visitors.

The tourist hotspot in west London, founded in 1759 and now a Unesco World Heritage Site, said on Friday it planned to cut operating costs by 10pc to salvage its finances.

Visitor numbers fell sharply during the summer, dropping from 5,800 per day when temperatures were 27C to just 2,800 when the thermometer hit 38C, figures show.

The extreme heat also forced parts of its historic glasshouses to close, while school visits were cancelled, depriving the gardens of income.

The cuts come after a rise in spending at Kew in recent years, with the average number of full-time staff rising almost 50pc over the past seven years to 1,312 full-time employees.

That has led to a near doubling of the wage bill over the same period, from £35.5m to £67.3m, with staff now accounting for roughly half of Kew’s costs.

Richard Deverell, Kew’s director, denied the problems were linked to an overexpansion and instead pointed to climate change.

Mr Deverell, who has been director since 2012, said the ballooning staffing numbers largely reflected temporary jobs funded through research grants and donations rather than permanent additions to the gardens’ operating costs.

He said around 900 employees were supported by Kew’s core operating budget, with a further 400 to 500 working on externally funded projects.

The chief said that increasingly frequent heatwaves threatened to undermine Kew’s finances by discouraging visitors during what has traditionally been its busiest season.

However, he acknowledged that climate change was only one of several pressures facing the attraction, alongside higher energy bills, National Insurance contributions, minimum wages and weak consumer confidence.

He said: “There are many factors buffeting Kew’s financial health. One of which is extreme heat.”

Kew’s latest accounts show that expenditure rose to £128m in the year to March, up from £118m the previous year, while income increased to £145m.

However, Mr Deverell argued that differences in the timing of funding for major projects distorted the accounts.

He said Kew had balanced its core operating budget each year for the past decade.

Mr Deverell said the savings would also help Kew double its contingency funding and establish an investment fund to support future income growth.

He said: “The 10pc cost reduction isn’t just about solving the problems we had this year. It’s trying to reset our finances more fundamentally to build much longer-term financial resilience.”

data.title: Landlords return to London as flat prices plunge
data.description:
Buy-to-let investors are starting to come back to London as flat prices plunge and rental yields rise sharply.

A combination of soaring rents and discounted purchase prices means landlords are buying flats in the capital at the fastest pace in years.

The share of London-based investors purchasing in the city has jumped from 34pc last year to an 11-year high of 39pc, according to Hamptons.

Guy Gittins, the chief executive of Foxtons, London’s biggest estate agent, said: “What we’ve seen in the last three months is that because of the capital sums that we’ve seen coming down, particularly on taller blocks, we have started to see the return of the rental investor in quite interesting numbers.”

Mr Gittins added: “I was in our Canary Wharf office four weeks ago and we went through the seven agreed sales that week. Five of them were to rental investors. I hadn’t seen that for the last seven years in London.”

Analysis by Hamptons shows gross rental yields on newly purchased London flats have soared to 7pc, up from 6pc last year and the highest level on record since Hamptons’ dataset began in 2015.

The share of landlord buyers getting 10pc yields on flats has more than doubled, rising from 7pc in 2025 to 15pc this year. It is the first time the proportion has been in double digits since at least 2015. Five years ago the share was just 1pc.

Aneisha Beveridge, the research director at Hamptons, said: “Higher yields seem to be tempting some investors back into parts of the London market, particularly where prices have adjusted but rents remain strong.”

The numbers suggest the Government’s buy-to-let crackdown – which began in 2016 with the introduction of a three-percentage-point stamp duty surcharge on additional properties, and has ramped up recently with Labour’s Renters’ Rights Act and John Healey’s Budget increase in tax rates on rental income – is starting to backfire in the capital.

Investors have been selling up for years, driving a shortage of supply that has sent rents soaring and triggered pain for the renters many of Labour’s policies were intended to help.

Now, investors are returning to the market to profit from the high rents, which continue to rise.

Office for National Statistics data show monthly rents in London in October were up by 3.7pc year-on-year and had soared by 31.2pc since the same month in 2022.

In contrast, prices of London flats, which is the market where buy-to-let investment is typically concentrated, were down by 6.3pc year-on-year in September, according to Land Registry figures. They have fallen by 10.6pc since their last peak in August 2022.

Falls are even steeper in the capital’s inner boroughs, where flat prices were down by 8.5pc year-on-year in September and have fallen by 12.6pc since their 2022 peak.

Adam Jennings, the head of residential at Chestertons, said: “Internally, we are starting to see property prices have got to a level where it is actually attractive from a yield perspective for investors to reinvest. Rents are high, prices are low.”

Mr Gittins added: “For the first time in my property career, we can sell a property to a rental investor with an 8pc, 9pc or 10pc yield in pretty much every regional patch [of London] – in central, north, south, east and west.

“When I was an estate agent selling properties for the first 10 years of my career in central London, I never sold a single property to a rental investor with more than a 3pc yield.”

data.title: Anthropic lacks ‘basic moral compass’, say publishers
data.description:
Anthropic’s cavalier approach to copyright shows the AI giant “lacks a basic moral compass”, news publishers have said.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents titles including The Telegraph, The Times and The Guardian, attacked the company after admissions in its stock market filing.

Anthropic, which went public on Thursday at a valuation of $1.5tn (£1.1tn), told investors it could not guarantee it would adhere to measures that prevented journalism from being used to train AI models.

The Claude maker said it took steps to abide by paywalls and a system known as robots.txt, which tells web crawlers what pages they can access, but that this “may not always be successful”.

Anthropic also acknowledged that it might not be able to verify whether the material it used to train its models was protected by copyright.

Theo Bamber, the chief executive of the NMA, said: “Anthropic’s IPO (initial public offering) filing confirms a chilling reality about how this new darling of the stock market operates.

“Paying for content should be a basic cost of doing business and investors should ask how long their new cash cow thinks it can go without paying its bills.

“If Anthropic’s lack of a basic moral compass does not give them pause for thought, the massive legal exposure should.”

Silicon Valley’s ‘hollow’ promises

Baroness Kidron, the crossbench peer and filmmaker who directed Bridget Jones: The Edge of Reason, said the filing showed AI companies’ promises to respect copyright were “hollow”.

She said: “The only thing that has compelled it to make this confession is the pursuit of money through its IPO. But our laws should not be a victim of their greed.”

Copyright has emerged as a major flashpoint in AI amid accusations tech companies have used vast troves of data to train their models without permission.

Dame Caroline Dinenage, the chairman of the Commons culture, media and sport committee, accused Silicon Valley firms last year of the “largest copyright heist” in history.

At the same time, the rise of chatbots and Google’s AI summaries is diverting readers away from news sites, leading to sharp drops in online traffic.

The Telegraph is among a number of British news outlets that have joined forces to stop AI giants from cashing in on their journalism.

Anthropic and rivals including ChatGPT maker OpenAI have relied on “fair use” principles under copyright law to date.

But in filings published before its stock market debut this week, Anthropic acknowledged that the legality of this approach had not been “authoritatively resolved” by courts in the US and around the world.

AI companies are facing a wave of lawsuits from publishers and rights holders about alleged copyright infringement, with The New York Times suing both OpenAI and Perplexity.

Anthropic itself was forced last year to pay $1.5bn to settle a copyright claim about its use of pirated books, with Harry Potter publisher Bloomsbury among those to receive a payout.

The filing revealed that the company faces two further lawsuits from publishers in Canada which allege their journalism was used to train Claude models.

Other outlets, including Rupert Murdoch’s News Corp and The New York Times, have opted to sign licensing deals with AI developers for the use of their content.

Anthropic acknowledged that if it could not rely on the fair use defence, it might be required to pay “significant fees” to obtain a licence.

In the UK, Labour is facing a backlash against its plans to water down copyright laws to allow AI companies to scrape data unless rights holders explicitly opt out.

Baroness Kidron added: “Anthropic is built in part on other people’s property.

“Ministers should read this filing and ask themselves who they were protecting when they refused to give creators basic transparency and whether there is any justification to refuse it now they see the abuse of our law in black and white.”

Anthropic has been contacted for comment.

data.title: What opening a joint bank account taught me about my relationship
data.description:
How do you and your partner deal with joint expenses? Let us know in the comments or email money@telegraph.co.uk*.

If you had told me a year ago that £1 doughnuts would test my relationship with my partner, I wouldn’t have believed it.

My boyfriend Alex and I have been together for two-and-a-half years, yet because work keeps us in separate cities, we have never lived together. Recently, however, we decided to take a different kind of “next step” in our relationship: opening a joint bank account.

There were practical reasons for this, but I was also curious to see how our relationship, as yet untested by more traditional milestones such as marriage, would handle an experiment such as this.

We both thought we knew each other’s attitudes to money, but creating even a relatively small shared pot compels you to turn abstract ideas about fairness, ownership and compromise into actual rules.

We agreed to put the same amount of money into the account as and when it needs topping up. Household items and food we buy when staying together are considered joint expenses, along with train tickets or petrol for travelling to see each other.

Our foray into shared finances was going swimmingly until one day, I got a notification from the bank saying that £1 had just been spent on our joint card. My partner walked in the door a few minutes later, excited because he had just found a pack of five doughnuts on sale for – you guessed it – £1.

This was something that had come up in our relationship before: Alex, a committed saver, is often content to buy or eat whatever is cheapest, while I am more of a food (and everything else) snob who would sooner spend a few extra pounds.

I wasn’t annoyed at the money, but it did puzzle me that he considered this a joint purchase when he was the only one going to be eating them. Fearful of being petty, I decided to let the issue lie.

Yet soon enough, the same question started appearing everywhere. If Alex wants the cheapest toilet paper while I would sooner spring for something softer, should he have to subsidise my preference? If we buy chocolate from the joint account but he eats most of it, is that really a shared expense?

We might have known what we were getting into. Research published by Starling Bank last year found that 76pc of surveyed couples argued about money regardless of how they managed their finances.

Becky Palmano, a 38-year-old production executive based in Jersey, faced similar issues when she first combined finances with her now-husband, Sam, also 38.

Initially, she tells me, they thought they were alike in how they approached money.

Once they began making financial decisions together, this turned out not to be the case: “My attitude is quite ‘live now’, which can occasionally become ‘spend now’, whereas Sam is more inclined to plan ahead, save and deliberate over bigger decisions like trips.”

The couple have devised a strategy for dealing with financial “missteps”, which they call “idiot tax”. The couple keep a shared savings pot of around £5,000 to cover the financial consequences of either of them doing something stupid.

“Recently, I booked Sam on to entirely the wrong flight. Idiot tax,” says Palmano. “The basic rule is that if it’s a genuine mistake, you’re allowed to be annoyed, but you don’t get to turn it into a huge argument about the money. Whoever has messed up has to hold their hands up, admit they’ve been an idiot and, ideally, not do it again.”

She also spoke of an incident early on in their relationship where a disastrous weekend away resulted in a series of costly financial blunders, including a last-minute hire car (which then got damaged) and a speeding fine.

Ultimately, they decided to split the damage 50-50 after realising that sometimes, trying to establish exactly whose expense something is “becomes more ridiculous than the expense itself”.

This was a trap I had already fallen into with my partner. After an absurd discussion where we tried to calculate who was subsidising more of the other’s spending, we resolved to continue splitting things equally and save ourselves the trouble of accounting for every difference in consumption and salary.

Admittedly, this isn’t something I usually agree with. I have always felt that it is best to split things equitably, so if your partner earns more than you, then what they pay in terms of rent and household expenses should reflect that gap.

Yet the difference between our salaries is small – I would estimate that Alex earns £5,000 more than me annually, although it’s difficult to know for certain as we both take on ad-hoc work.

We agreed that for the time being, our relationship would be best served by letting the little things go.

Tom Desborough, a financial planner at Paradigm Norton, suggests that those with different attitudes to spending are not inherently incompatible. He finds most couples are willing to compromise a bit because it’s part of being in a loving relationship.

If you want to avoid being blindsided by your partner’s spending habits, however, he recommends asking more holistic questions early on in the relationship. For example, where do you see your life in 10 or 20 years’ time, or if you won the lottery, what would you do?

You may already know that you are both savers, but what you are saving your money for is just as important.

Desborough also recommends a “yours, mine and ours” approach, rather than pooling everything. It is a system Eduardo Gomes, 38, and his wife Carla, 44, eventually arrived at, although it took an expensive accidental purchase to get them there.

When they moved from Brazil to London, they combined their finances to cover rent and household costs, using a single credit card.

During Covid, Eduardo found an auction website and placed bids on five coffee machines, unexpectedly winning all five at a cost of around £1,000. Understandably, his wife wasn’t pleased. He managed to sell four of the machines for a profit, but they have since switched to having both joint and separate accounts.

Now, Gomes says, they have learned from each other’s attitudes; Carla has taught him the importance of having a savings buffer, especially as she now works part-time to spend more time with their young daughter, and he has encouraged her to be more adventurous.

“Ultimately, we complement each other’s spending behaviours,” he says.

This was another lesson Alex and I learned. We could have gone back and forth for hours over whose attitude to money was better, but ultimately, if we wanted to move forward, we needed to accept that there wasn’t going to be an outcome where either of us “wins”.

In that sense, combining even a small part of our finances became a useful trial run for the long-term relationship we hope to have. We might have spent ages debating fairness and compromise in the abstract, but we needed to put those ideas into practice to see how we would build a financial life together.

Of course, compromising over £1 doughnuts is one thing. Making bigger decisions down the line will be considerably harder. The important thing is that we understand each other’s respective money attitudes before we try.

data.title: Talk of public control is ‘kryptonite’ to investment, Burnham warned
data.description:
Andy Burnham is fuelling fears of renationalisation that are “kryptonite to investment”, the boss of Britain’s biggest business group has warned.

Rain Newton-Smith, the chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), will on Monday urge the Prime Minister to reassure investors that private companies could remain involved in major projects under Labour.

In a speech to politicians and major business leaders at the CBI’s annual conference, she will warn that the Prime Minister needs to show that he “wants private capital at the table – not heading for the exit”.

It comes as Mr Burnham has repeatedly called for greater public control of what he describes as the “essentials of life”.

“To some, ‘public control’ sounds like code for renationalisation. That is kryptonite to investment,” Ms Newton-Smith will say, adding that Britain can only escape its “financial straitjacket” by backing business.

While the chief executive will stress that the CBI does not believe wholesale renationalisation is on the cards, she will call for greater clarity from ministers.

The demand promises to set up a clash with the Government. Minutes after Ms Newton-Smith speaks, Louise Haigh, a key ally of Mr Burnham, will tell the conference that Britain needs greater public control of water and energy companies.

She will say that Britain’s privatised utilities have failed and that public control is “not anti-business”.

Ms Haigh will also attack overseas ownership of UK utilities, saying that foreign governments own “significant stakes in our water, electricity and gas networks with returns paid to their taxpayers”.

Mr Burnham is preparing to unveil a 10-year plan next month with more details about his public control model.

He has signalled he will take action on water, transport, housing and energy in a move he claims will bring down household costs and put public services before private profit.

However, the debacle at Thames Water shows how damaging this can be.

Before entering No 10, Mr Burnham had pledged to exert public control of the beleaguered water company, but has since failed to come up with a plan to bring it under government ownership.

It is thought that the cost of nationalising key infrastructure would run into the hundreds of billions of pounds, with estimates showing that a state-led rescue of Thames Water would cost the taxpayer around £2.4bn.

The Conservative Party has repeatedly ruled out state ownership of utility companies if it returns to power.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Labour think nationalisation is a magic wand for every industry and every problem. The only trick they know is splurging ever more taxpayers’ money.”

The conference will also feature leaders from all of the main political parties, including Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader; Nigel Farage, Reform UK’s leader; Ed Davey from the Liberal Democrats; and the Green Party’s Zack Polanski, alongside Alan Milburn, the worklessness tsar.

In her speech, Mrs Badenoch is also set to accuse Labour of securing a “terrible” deal with the EU, saying Mr Burnham is underselling Britain’s potential by binding the country to the trading bloc.

The Prime Minister has hailed the prospect of a 0.4pc boost to GDP by establishing closer ties with his reset deal, unveiled on Friday, but Mrs Badenoch will say he is “thinking way too small” and should be focusing on boosting trade with Asia.

Mr Farage will also warn that closer ties with Brussels would be a “disaster” for British businesses.

However, Ms Newton-Smith will urge Mr Burnham to push for a “closer relationship” with the EU, saying Brexit was a “wrong turn for our economy”.

A spokesman for the Cabinet Office said: “Public control is about partnership with business, not renationalisation.

“We’re backing business in a real partnership targeted at key sectors – transport, energy, housing and water – with clear rules, to stop essential services ripping off the public while giving investors the certainty and confidence they need to invest.”
