data.title: Britain’s banks have turned into Big Brother
data.description:
A smooth-running banking sector is essential to keep the wheels of the economy turning. But Britain’s banking sector is anything but smooth. Try to open a new bank account and you may well be refused.

Even when people and businesses can open an account, they could face years of faultless operation before having the facilities withdrawn at short notice, leaving them high and dry.

We might be inclined to blame the banks for being so obtuse, but it is the indiscriminate threat of fines levied by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) and our demand for recompense if we are scammed or defrauded which has created the level of twitchiness from banks that we now see. It all adds up to a culture of “debanking”.

Millions of bank customers are encountering an increasingly intrusive reality of modern personal finance: unexpected, urgent demands from their banks for deep personal financial information.

Failure to comply within tight deadlines carries a serious penalty: immediate account restriction or permanent termination.

I experienced this myself recently at the hands of a major high street bank with whom I’ve held a secondary bank account for 15 years.

Nothing had changed with my banking use and volumes across those years. I had to provide 34 PDF files of information to “prove” every source of income, and practically every asset I owned, with an explanation as to how I came by the capital to buy such assets.

I was given three weeks to provide the information, with telephone chasers twice a week, weekly emails and texts to chivvy me along.

The implied threats within their emails were chilling: “If we haven’t heard from you by X, we might need to restrict access to your account(s). This means you won’t be able to access money or make regular or one-off payments from your account(s). This could include mortgage payments or other standing orders and direct debits.”

You may ask why I didn’t tell them to do one.

It was certainly in my mind, but I’d opened a trust account for my young daughter with them some years ago and was more mindful of the loss of that account. The pain and aggravation of opening an alternative children’s account made me comply with their threats.

It was truly foul. I felt abused and belittled.

An increasing number of routine, low-value electronic payments now require unblocking, necessitating a lengthy phone call to the bank’s “fraud line” – which usually goes unanswered for 15 minutes or more. Then you need to give an explanation, such as that paying a plumber or builder is routine for you, and that you have not been coerced into making the payment.

This is followed by an exercise in being spoken to like a child from a prepared script of banking dos and don’ts.

I have no hard evidence, but anecdotally, payments to banks such as Monzo, Starling and Revolut seem to have a higher likelihood of being blocked. Is this the closed shop of the big banks lashing out?

When challenged, financial institutions invariably cite regulatory obligations under FCA supervision and anti-money-laundering legislation.

Banks are legally required to maintain ongoing “customer due diligence”, but little guidance is offered about what is reasonable.

At the heart of the problem is that customers are not believed.

Outside the private banking world and with the increasing closure of high-street branches, no personal banking relationships exist. Common sense has disappeared to algorithmic risk-scoring.

I can fully agree with inquiries over remittances from high-risk foreign countries, but surely such levels of due diligence should not be required for domestic transfers between regulated UK financial institutions?

And all the while, the network of cash-laundering high-street “businesses” cruises along unhindered. It is yet more evidence of a failing Britain.

data.title: Drivers face delays for compensation after FCA counting error
data.description:
Drivers face further delays in receiving compensation for the £9.1bn car finance scandal after the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) admitted a series of data errors.

The City watchdog confirmed on Thursday that it had mistakenly calculated how it categorised a small group of loan agreements that had been used to work out how much compensation some drivers were owed.

It said the effect on the average individual compensation package would be less than £10.

The FCA previously announced in March that the average motorist mis-sold car finance would receive £829 from its redress scheme, which would cover 12.1 million historic vehicle loan deals.

However, the City watchdog also warned that the calculation errors could disrupt ongoing litigation over the scheme, which could mean further delays to payouts.

Much of the compensation initiative has already been suspended until the Upper Tribunal hears a string of challenges to the redress scheme in February next year, brought by the likes of Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz.

But proceedings could also be disrupted further.

Katie Stephen, a partner at City law firm Norton Rose Fulbright, said: “There is a potential domino effect here.

“Two of the challengers are due to serve expert evidence imminently, followed by the FCA’s evidence in December and January, meetings between the experts and written arguments ahead of the February hearing.

“If the first of those deadlines moves, there is a risk that subsequent stages also have to move.

“It does not automatically follow that the February hearing will be delayed and the parties will likely try to make up any lost time but there is not a great deal of room in the existing timetable.”

Volkswagen Financial Services (VWFS), Mercedes-Benz Financial Services and Crédit Agricole Auto Finance have all challenged the scheme, as well as Consumer Voice, a campaign group supported by Courmacs Legal, one of the largest mass-claim motor finance law firms.

A spokesman for VWFS said it understood that the errors were related to a foundational dataset that underpinned the design of the FCA’s scheme and that they could have broader implications.

“We have requested urgent clarification on the impact of these errors and will work diligently with our lawyers to understand any impact,” the spokesman added.

The FCA said it had also asked Barclays to pause its plans to make early settlement offers to drivers until it worked out the full implications of the miscalculations.

The watchdog apologised for the further uncertainty for consumers and firms created by the mistakes.

data.title: How English churches became an endangered species
data.description:
In the past decade, more than 3,500 churches in the UK have closed. Some buildings have been left empty, while others have been deconsecrated, sold and turned into quirky homes marketed for their “period details”. It’s a trend that shows no sign of stopping. More than 900 churches are on Historic England’s “Heritage at Risk” register, and the Church of Scotland has plans to close as many as 40 per cent of its churches.

The reasons for these closures are depressingly predictable. A decline in faith results in fewer parishioners; those parishioners then require fewer priests to minister them. But sometimes the reason is more structural. Congregations often can’t afford the repairs that their ancient building requires (a problem made worse since places of worship lost their VAT exemption in April 2026), and so the church is simply left to rot. It’s a sad fate for the buildings which, in author and conservator Rachel Morley’s words, constitute “England’s greatest architectural endowment”. To ignore their plight would be to commit “an irreparable act of national self-harm”.

Named after John Betjeman’s favourite pastime, Morley’s Church Crawling is a charming, meandering journey through some of England’s 15,000 parish churches and more than a millennium of their history. Morley wants us to think about what “churches are”, distinct from the religious purpose they were built for. It’s a gamble of an argument – and one that initially seems to risk leaving the heart out of the book.

The fact that so many ancient churches have survived – and continue to do so – is partly down to an ingenious twist in English churches’ construction. Their geological foundations are often specific to their location, with churches in the south-west made from granite, some in Brentor, Devon, from volcanic debris and “petrified lava pillows”, and some from flint in East Anglia, where that rock reigns supreme. 

Some clever masons developed a way of spelling out letters and monograms in flint; from “M-A-R-I-A” for the Virgin Mary, to the rather less parsable “A-N-SJ-B-S-T-M-S-A-H-K-R” (which apparently stands for a lengthy phrase declaring that the chancel of a church in Blythburgh, Suffolk, was rebuilt in the name of St John the Baptist, the Holy Trinity, St Mary and St Anne).

Others still bear the scars of the Reformation. One, St Catherine’s in Ludham, Norfolk, has both sides of the debate on its walls: a painted 16th-century rood (a large crucifix) now hangs with its back to a canvas of the Royal Arms (Mary I demanded the rood, Elizabeth I the coat of arms). Though the congregation was forced to cover up Mary’s rood with Elizabeth’s arms within a handful of years, they later kept both ornaments stuffed in a void in the church walls, where they remained until a group of Victorian archaeologists found them. As Morley’s stories reveal, the Reformation was not one moment of rupture for life in the Church but a series of ordinances from on high – followed with what was more or less zeal by the parishioners.

Morley is the director of the charity Friends of Friendless Churches, a role that allows her to write about buildings inaccessible to most. In one of the book’s closing chapters, we hear of her visit to the besieged churches in the “Stanford Training Area” (Stanta) in Norfolk, an area that was cleared for wartime training in 1942, and never demilitarised afterwards. The villages have been decimated and demolished, but the churches stand – surrounded by chicken-wire, with their stones and glass damaged by rounds of live fire. Morley visited to discuss the possibility of better care for the buildings, but we don’t hear of any success.

Church Crawling is at its best when Morley dwells on tangible, individual details of church buildings: their stonework, their floors, the tiny motifs in their stained glass. This attention, ironically, is a story of faith. In one of the most heartfelt episodes of the book, Morley recounts Coventry’s “Night of Terror” in 1940, when the city was engulfed in fires from the Blitz. The vicar of Holy Trinity, Graham Clitheroe, fought the flames for hours, single-handedly securing his church’s survival and its medieval doom painting. Holy Trinity is now the only medieval church left complete in the city after the bombing destroyed so many others, including Coventry Cathedral.

What emerges from these disparate stories is a rich evocation of England’s material culture. Churches are part of our architectural furniture, but their history is one of continual change: of Norman origins, medieval additions and modern alterations. And despite all the dilapidation and decay, Church Crawling is as much a tale of hope as it is of doom. So much can change in a church’s lifetime; for some ruins, a revival might be just around the corner.

★★★★☆

data.title: Veterans forced to take 5am rail replacement bus to Remembrance Sunday
data.description:
Veterans have been offered a rail replacement bus at nearly 5am to reach Remembrance Sunday events in London.

Major Christopher McLean, 67, from Wiltshire, said the arrangements were “not good enough” and would prevent fellow veterans attending memorials.

In an email seen by The Telegraph, the Royal British Legion warned Cenotaph Parade ticket-holders that rail engineering works would bring disruption on Nov 8.

The charity advised veterans that South Western Railway and Network Rail Wessex were offering limited one-way bus travel from Winchester and Salisbury railway stations that were departing at 4.45am to arrive at London Waterloo at 8am.

Scheduled replacement bus services are also operating, requiring changes between rail and bus services to arrive in London on time.

Major McLean, who lives outside Salisbury, told The Telegraph that the disruption meant he would have to get up at 3.45am, which was not ideal at his age.

“No one seems to have thought this through,” he told The Telegraph, adding: “If I had planned like that in my Army logistics career, I would have been sacked.”

Veterans forced to ‘make other arrangements’

Major McLean said that veterans would be prevented attending events in the capital because of the disruption.

He said: “Lots of us are in our 70s. What about the implications for people who are infirm? It’s not good enough. Most of the guys I know are going to have to make other arrangements.

“Luckily, I can go up the night before and stay with relatives in Surrey. If I hadn’t had family there, I would have pulled out.

“Others are looking at paying for two nights in a London hotel, which is expensive. The Royal British Legion does a great job getting this all together, but the wider logistics haven’t been considered properly.”

Veterans would have been able to leave closer to 7am if the trains were running. This would still have allowed them enough time to arrive in Whitehall, pass through police security procedures and form up on the Cenotaph for 10.30am.

Major McLean said the rail disruption was the latest woe to be bestowed on veterans.

He said: “Prosecutions of veterans, underfunding of defence – it’s one thing after another, which is really upsetting this community. This is the latest mark of disrespect.”

Veteran’s fiercely oppose Labour’s Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, which is currently in the House of Lords, arguing that it does not adequately protect former service members.

Col Richard Kemp, a retired British Army officer who served from 1977 to 2006, criticised the lack of foresight by the railway operators.

“This is probably the most important day of the year when people can come together and pay respects to the war dead,” he said, adding: “It should be given priority above other events.

“Veterans should be treated with the utmost respect, including by the railway companies. This clearly isn’t good enough.”

Last month, the Government announced that it was extending free railway travel on Remembrance weekend, which currently covers serving military staff, veterans and one next of kin of a service-person who died while serving.

However, networks across the country will be disrupted by engineering work on Nov 7 and 8.

South Western Railway, the first operator to be renationalised by Labour in May 2025, apologised to veterans whose journeys would be affected.

A spokesman said: “South Western Railway is proud of its commitment to the Armed Forces community and this year received the Ministry of Defence Gold Award.

“Unfortunately, long-planned and essential engineering works this weekend mean veterans will need to use a combination of train and rail replacement services to travel to London Waterloo.

“We investigated whether the engineering works could be rescheduled, but this would have meant deferring essential track maintenance to maintain the long-term safety and reliability of the railway.”

A spokesman for the Royal British Legion said: “We’ve worked with the rail authorities to contact veterans affected by planned engineering works so they know a rail replacement service has been arranged.”

data.title: Twelve flights diverted across Europe after bomb threats
data.description:
Twelve flights have been diverted across Europe following a series of bomb threats.

Thursday’s disruption comes days after similar incidents in which eight planes, including three from the UK, were grounded over what Britain dismissed as a “malicious hoax”.

Three of Thursday’s incidents involved flights bound for Italy.

An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to Normandy following a bomb alert, the French prime minister’s office said.

The office of Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, said all 151 passengers and six crew members were safe, and that military bomb defusal teams were examining the plane.

A Finnair flight bound for Helsinki landed in Rome after a threat was reported on board, while a Wizz Air service from Milan Malpensa to Warsaw was diverted to Vienna.

A Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at Zaventem airport in Belgium after the crew received a “suspicious report concerning a flight to Brussels airport”.

Three more aircraft were forced to land at airports in Bulgaria following bomb threats. 

Two of the planes – travelling from Copenhagen and Madrid respectively – landed in Sofia, the broadcaster bTV, citing the interior minister, reported.

A third aircraft, flying from London, landed in Plovdiv, according to reports. Four planes flying to Prague had been the subject of bomb threats and were preparing to land, according to Czech police. 

A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest was also targeted, Romanian intelligence services said.

On Thursday morning, Spanish authorities said three flights at Madrid were affected by hoax threats.

None of the threats reported this week have been found to be genuine, despite triggering dozens of unplanned landings as well and escorts by fighter jets.

The EU’s transport commissioner said it was “too early to draw conclusions” on whether Thursday’s spate of bomb threats were linked.

Apostolos Tzitzikostas said in a message posted on LinkedIn that he had asked EU security authorities “to cooperate closely with airport operators, airlines and law enforcement authorities” over the bomb threats.

On Tuesday, at least seven planes were subjected to threats. A flight to Sofia was similarly affected on Monday.

An airport in Warsaw was briefly shut and the Italian air force accompanied one of the flights to Rome. An Israel-bound cruise ship was also searched for bombs in Greece.

A British Government spokesman told The Telegraph that the threats against the UK flights had been a “malicious hoax”, though it was not clear how they had been orchestrated.

Speculation quickly centred on Moscow, with a former MI6 intelligence officer telling The Telegraph that it was his first thought when he learned of the bomb threats, which he said fitted “a pattern of behaviour” by the Kremlin.

The flight disruption follows a week of chaos, with dozens of supermarket fridges across Europe hacked on Monday. The attacks caused large amounts of food to spoil after hackers gained remote access to in-store fridge units and turned up their temperatures, in some cases to as much as 80C.

Hackers also targeted France’s national blood bank, raising the temperature of its cold storage rooms to boiling point.

Facilities at Coolworld were heated to 110C overnight on Sunday after hackers gained access to the temperature settings remotely, Le Canard enchaîné reported. The rooms are normally kept at -30C to preserve donor blood samples.

An on-duty technician detected the unusual rise in temperatures. France’s health ministry said there had been no consequences for patients and no plasma had been destroyed.

The Kremlin said European media accusations of Russian involvement in ‌cyber attacks on supermarkets were not backed up by any evidence.

Dmitry ⁠Peskov, a Kremlin spokesman, told reporters on Thursday: “These are absurd claims. As always, they are backed up by absolutely ‌no reasoning, no evidence whatsoever, and yet here we have ⁠such ⁠baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything.”

However, pro-Russian hackers have claimed responsibility for the cyber attacks on fridges.

The pro-Russian hacking collective NoName057(16) claimed to have worked with Z-Pentest, another pro-Russian hacker group, to launch the attack.

A video claiming responsibility for the attack was posted on Telegram, according to the Danish media outlet DR.

In the video, titled Operation Chronicle: Danfoss, the hackers claimed to have “dealt a crushing blow to Danfoss and Dixell XWEB equipment”.

Danfoss and Dixell XWEB were the refrigeration companies targeted in the cyber attack.

“We didn’t even need malware for that. We just exploited the systems’ built-in features,” the hackers said.

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: Are Poundland’s owners thick-skinned or just thick?
data.description:
It was less than four hours before The Telegraph revealed Poundland had collapsed into administration that sources close to the sale process were still insisting that three buyers were in the running.

Such bluster is often part of a protracted mergers and acquisitions (M&A) process, but on this occasion it typified a sale process that has been deeply flawed from the off. With a cast of City advisers as long as your arm, the spin surrounding Poundland’s downfall has at times been laughable.

It started in September when Gordon Brothers, Poundland’s US owner, tasked restructuring experts at Alvarez & Marsal – the firm that oversaw fruitless attempts to sell failed broadband business TalkTalk – with launching an “auction”.

At the time, it was said that Gordon Brothers was seeking a sale after receiving “a number of unsolicited approaches”, most notably from Poundstretcher owner Fortress.

Confidence was such that the firm’s advisers even suggested a deal could be struck before the end of October.

If only. Three months later and administrators were finally called in, to the detriment of more than 10,000 workers who now face losing their jobs before Christmas.

For many employees, it will no doubt come as a remarkable shock after recent media briefings talked up the prospect of “last-gasp” rescue offers, largely from people you’ve never heard of.

Among the list of suitors were a 23-year-old cigar aficionado who’d never bought a retailer, a mystery cash-and-carry wholesaler from the Middle East and an ex-German journalist whose office appears to be housed above a florist in the rural town of Grünheide.

Of course, Gordon Brothers’ latest PR advisers insisted on Wednesday that “our thoughts are with Poundland colleagues”, as they recognised “how difficult the continued uncertainty is for them”.

They sought to stress that every avenue had been explored to secure a sale during an “extensive three-month M&A process”, blaming “several years of instability” and inflationary pressures for leaving the chain vulnerable.

However, unsurprisingly, little was said about why Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for £1 last year after acquiring other distressed companies including Laura Ashley and LK Bennett, had rejected several multimillion-pound offers.

Nor did they mention that they were holding out for repayment of a £30m loan, all of which had to be paid upfront.

The spin hasn’t ended even after the final nail has been hammered into Poundland’s coffin, which will inevitably once again raise hopes among worried shop-floor staff.

Idris Mohammed, a bidder whose online profile was entirely non-existent until last week, claimed on Thursday that the “intense media coverage and political pressure” was to blame for the botched sale.

If only the Government had played ball, stumped up taxpayer cash and sought to “share the risk”, he said while insisting he was still interested in buying the business out of administration. Remind me, Idris, who are you again?

As one well-informed executive, who had long predicted Poundland’s administration, said to me over the weekend: “Gordon Brothers is taking the p--- out of everyone, especially the management and staff.

“They have been putting all sorts of stuff out there to make it look like they’re making an effort to sell. It’s shocking behaviour.”

The expectation now is that Westminster will turn its gaze on the US investment firm, as ministers reckon with the biggest high-street collapse since BHS in 2016.

As well as leaving dozens of suppliers out of pocket, Poundland’s failure will also entangle Andy Burnham, owing to the fact that its biggest distribution centre is located in his Makerfield constituency.

As administrators at Alix Partners take control, break-up of the business is now the most likely option. This will ensure there is no certainty over any of Poundland’s 600 stores or its Walsall head office.

Liam Byrne, chairman of the Commons business and trade committee, has already called Mark Newton-Jones, Gordon Brothers’ European head, to appear for another hearing in a scramble for answers over the crisis.

One can only hope that Byrne doesn’t blow it by allowing the session to be held in private, as was the case two weeks ago when Gordon Brothers came out unscathed.

But whether any of the highly paid executives at Gordon Brothers or Alvarez & Marsal will care is another matter. It is worth remembering that this isn’t their first public-relations disaster.

Look no further than Newton-Jones’s track record in retail. The veteran executive, whose spinners recently arranged for him to attend friendly sit-downs with selected journalists, once put more than 1,000 people out of work at Very Group by shutting down a string of regional call-centres.

Yet rather than burying this painful memory, Newton-Jones later told a retail conference that workers affected by the redundancies had burned effigies of him on the street.

So for all the inevitable political backlash and tales of worker woe before Christmas, I wouldn’t hold my breath for any sleepless nights among staff in Gordon Brothers’ HQ.

In the words of one City source: “I can’t decide whether they are thick-skinned or simply just thick.”

data.title: Labour’s ‘unfair’ bank tax will have consequences, warns JP Morgan boss
data.description:
The boss of JP Morgan has warned that John Healey’s bank tax raid will have consequences for Britain, as he vowed to set an “example” by finding ways to claw back the levy.

In a veiled threat to the Government, Jamie Dimon said he wanted politicians to “understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.

Mr Dimon lashed out at the Chancellor after he temporarily doubled the surcharge on bank profits above £100m from 3pc to 6pc during his maiden Budget to provide “immediate support on energy bills”.

He said that any move to offset the bank tax would be “more in sorrow” than in anger, but failed to specify how he would claw back the costs, as first reported by the Financial Times.

The Wall Street banking giant expects to pay between £100m to £150m because of Mr Healey’s higher surcharge.

Mr Dimon’s latest comments will renew scrutiny of JP Morgan’s proposals for a new £3bn headquarters in Canary Wharf.

The bank has not suggested any reversal to the tower’s development but it previously stressed that the project would depend on “a continuing positive business environment in the UK”.

The latest surcharge is levied in addition to the top rate of corporation tax, which now stands at 25pc.

That means the biggest banks in Britain now face a total tax rate of 31pc – the highest level since at least 2015.

Following the Budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimated that the higher tax rate will bring in an extra £1.5bn for the Treasury.

However, it also claimed that the UK would lose roughly £190m of profits as a result of the tax rise.

Mr Dimon has been among the staunchest critics of the policy, with the bank previously claiming that it has paid £5.5bn in bank taxes since 2011.

In July, he said there would be “adverse consequences” if the Government targeted lenders with fresh windfall taxes to help fund his spending plans.

“I always thought it was wrong,” he said. “We’re a great citizen [in the UK]. We hire people there. We want to be bigger there. We train people there. We hire veterans there.

“So if a government decides to do it, there’s nothing I can do, but it will over time cause decisions made that they may not like.”

JP Morgan declined to comment.
